product_7.description:
General Information
Buzz, buzz, buzz, little bee buzzes around
As pollinating insects, bees are invaluable in the global ecology. They are so useful that humans even keep honeybees, which produce valuable honey and beeswax. The importance of bees for maintaining biodiversity, for yields and thus also for feeding humans is so great that, in view of the "bee die-off" observed worldwide, the UN General Assembly addressed them and declared May 20 "World Bee Day" in 2017. A flower without a bee? Not only would we miss their buzzing and humming - life on Earth would simply be unrecognizable.
Some species form states and perform amazing dances to communicate. Depending on the task, the bees of a bee colony have different life expectancies. If a (honey) bee queen can live two to five years, a worker bee as a summer bee lives on average only four to five weeks, as a winter bee she can reach an age of several months. These bees, however, are felted by hand from pure New Zealand (and thus animal-friendly obtained) virgin wool and can therefore delight you far longer: not only in the midst of the branches and flowers of your vase arrangement, but also as an adornment of a small gift, as a decoration of your set table or simply as small, lovable lucky charms.

product_10.description:
General Information
Long-lasting Easter branch. Lasting nature conservation
Lastingly decorative: hand-felted from pure new wool, these willow catkin twigs are permanently fresh and budding and look just as fluffy as their natural role models, the catkins of the willow. The felt-wrapped wire branches not only provide a stable arrangement in the vase, but also lend themselves to other decorative ideas, for example for gift wrapping or decorating the Easter breakfast table.
After all, an Easter without pussy willows wouldn't be a real Easter - you wouldn't deny the Easter bunny the Easter eggs. The willow branches with their furry buds owe their significance to Christian tradition. Every year on Palm Sunday, Christians commemorate Jesus' entry into Jerusalem: according to tradition, the jubilant crowds laid out the Messiah's path with palm fronds. As palms do not grow in Europe (at least not voluntarily), the willow, which buds as early as March, was chosen for church decorations and processions, especially in Roman Catholic regions. Today, however, this tradition has its pitfalls, as the native willows (Salix caprea) are now a protected species. And for good reason: as early bloomers, willows are an important bee pasture, providing bees, bumblebees, butterflies and many other insects with the first vital food after winter. These felted willow catkins are a beautiful alternative that can also make nature conservationists smile - all the more so as you can arrange the twigs into an attractive bouquet throughout the spring and again the following year.

It belongs to the family. The Easter rabbit
Even the Easter Bunny can't be everywhere at once. That's why he will be happy to have a little wild rabbit: After all, it belongs to the family, can support him helpfully and represent the bunny here and there in the Easter decorations. product_22.description:
General Information
Upcycling. The cellulose egg
Something that has stood the test of time (and more than just hits the nerve of its time) survives over time and may eventually become a tradition. That's what happened to the Easter bunny, that's what happened to the Easter egg - and it's a similar story with the process developed around a hundred years ago, according to which these Easter eggs are turned by hand in Thuringia. For those who are now wondering, because Thuringia is better known for its artistic craftsmanship in glass and porcelain or for its woodworking, yes, these eggs are actually made from absorbent cotton (cellulose). This means that Thuringia as a production location is closer than the first impression suggests: Cellulose is obtained from wood, mostly from sawmill residue - and we are back to the traditional material and optimal upcycling. An immersion bath in dyed gelatine hardens the absorbent cotton Easter eggs and gives them their decorative base color. The stylized flower motifs are also dabbed on by hand using fine needles - making each Easter egg a small, delicate one-off.
The Egg and the Easter Celebrations.
Which came first: the rabbit or the egg? At Easter, we can make an unqualified case for the egg: Since the earliest beginnings of Christianity, the egg has been a symbol of fertility; it stands for new life and the resurrection of Christ. The Easter bunny, by contrast, had to prevail against illustrious competitors before it could establish itself as the exclusive egg supplier, depending on the region: the fox, the cuckoo and the stork – or even against the church bells flying home from Rome. Of course, not only the egg itself but also its colouring has a special significance. In the sphere of influence of the Orthodox Church, you found traditionally eggs dyed exclusively in red – in Christian symbolism, red stands for the blood of Christ. Over time and regionally differentiated, especially the Roman Catholic Church added other colours and significant meanings, for example, white symbolizing purity, yellow representing wisdom, and orange signifying endurance and strength.
Besides the festive-decorative purpose, there once was a thoroughly functional purpose that led to the dyeing of eggs (and, at the same time, to the tradition of hard-boiled Easter eggs): The peasants of the Middle Ages dyed their own eggs red to distinguish them from those they had to hand over to their landlord. What’s more, farmers preserved eggs by boiling them during the forty-day fasting period, when it was not allowed to eat eggs. Dyeing the different batches of eggs in one colour each helped colour-coding them before storing. The coding gave the farmers an overview of the growing supply of eggs and was an early form of best-before date. One could easily tell which batch of eggs comprised the oldest and was first in line for consumption.

product_26.description:
General Information
Lace art on wood crafts
Lace doilies may not be everyone's cup of tea, but a "lacey" decoration very much so. Filigree lace patterns enjoy a long tradition in Erzgebirge folk art, and so these Easter eggs are also turned from the solid wood of hornbeam and decorated with the lace motif by precise pad printing. The dots around each egg are finally painted on by hand. The sextet comes from a Seiffener manufactory, in which their craftsman father the turning and turning, carving and grinding was laid as it were in the cradle: Wolfgang Werner was born into a long-established family of toy makers. In addition to his moving constructions - such as swing figures, pendulum riders and running animals - the experienced toymaker also likes to take traditional pendants like these out of the lathe. In the Easter bouquet, the Easter eggs make themselves just as decorative as a colorful decoration of the festive table or a small Easter gift.
Folk art from the Erzgebirge. Seiffen
The fact that a famous wood art developed in the originally densely forested Erzgebirge is not only explained by the availability of the material. As a branch of industry, handicrafts became all the more important as the local mining industry rapidly lost resources and profitability. Folk art slipped into this gap, which mining - no less than Christmas - still shaped with numerous motifs. A center of wood art emerged around Seiffen, where one of the first specialized trade schools was founded in 1853 to promote handicrafts. In the so-called Toy Corner, small and large craft businesses still produce the classics of the folk art of the Erzgebirge: from hoop animals and smoking men to miner figures and nutcrackers to candle arches and wing pyramids.

product_39.description:
General Information
Spiritual harmony
Two customs, one from Christianity, the other from Buddhism, come together in these decorative Easter eggs:
In Sri Lanka, which is predominantly Buddhist, it is customary to bring a flower offering (pupphapuja) to the temple as a sign of respect and reverence. Flowers upon flowers, often lotus blossoms, are carried to the Buddha - when the blossoms begin to wither, they are disposed of by the priests. All the flowers? Not at all. Zero waste is the credo of the Danish company Lübech Living, which has entered into an agreement with a number of Sri Lankan temples. As a result, Lübech Living not only has waste paper processed as part of a women's initiative in Sri Lanka, but the flower offerings to be disposed of are also given a new purpose.
Flower by flower, leaf by leaf, is carefully plucked apart by hand and added to the pulp made from paper offcuts. The resulting discreet "Lotus Paper" is simple, yet robust, dimensionally stable and versatile, as is the case with these handmade decorative Easter eggs from the OOhh collection - and, en passant, two beliefs are harmoniously brought together: The (lotus) blossom as a Buddhist symbol of transience adorns the (Easter) egg as a Christian symbol of resurrection.
We offer this unusual Easter decoration as a set: with four Easter eggs in two sizes.

product_44.description:
General Information
Ready for the family business
They are, as it were, bunny youngsters - which is particularly evident when they stand next to the big Easter bunny from the same Seiffen workshop - but they are clearly already willing to help out in the family-run delivery service. Well, one of them might be a little more attentive (sharpened spoons), the other perhaps a little more reserved (spoons laid out). Either way, the two Easter bunnies owe their eloquent expression not only to their body language but also to the skill with which the striking grain of the ash wood has been incorporated into the design. Turned from solid ash wood, the grain expressively follows the contours of the figures and makes them (not only) decorative helpers in the family business.
Folk art from the Erzgebirge. Seiffen
The fact that a famous wood art developed in the originally densely forested Erzgebirge is not only explained by the availability of the material. As a branch of industry, handicrafts became all the more important as the local mining industry rapidly lost resources and profitability. Folk art slipped into this gap, which mining - no less than Christmas - still shaped with numerous motifs. A center of wood art emerged around Seiffen, where one of the first specialized trade schools was founded in 1853 to promote handicrafts. In the so-called Toy Corner, small and large craft businesses still produce the classics of the folk art of the Erzgebirge: from hoop animals and smoking men to miner figures and nutcrackers to candle arches and wing pyramids.

product_46.description:
General Information
Glass in glass. Uniquely fused
A small family business in Budapest produces these Easter eggs using traditional glassblowing techniques. First, glass tubes are drawn into blanks in front of the flame. Colored, finely ground glass - the glass granulate - is sprinkled into the resulting hot, viscous glass mass and distributed in the soft glass mass. Finally, the blank and glass granules are also fused together in front of the flame, creating the characteristic streaks of color; the egg is formed freely and the hanging loop is artfully pulled out of the glass.
Due to the random distribution of the colored glass particles, each glass Easter egg shines with a slightly different pattern and shimmers in a unique way in the light of the spring sun, in your Easter branches as well as in your window decoration.

product_61.description:
General Information
Play with me. Dance with me. Sing with me
Singing along to a song at the top of your lungs, listening spellbound to an adventure story, wiggling your body rhythmically and practicing what you will soon be able to call "dancing" - you can't do it without music and stories. And because children need their freedom and like to discover this exciting world of music and stories on their own, there is Hörbert, the MP3 player.
Simply powerful. Handmade for children's hands
The materials and workmanship make it clear: Hörbert is made for children's impetuous hands - carefully crafted by hand. The robust solid wood frame, made from local copper beech, is impressive at first glance. The front panel made of strong poplar plywood is neatly glued to the frame, while solid steel screws secure the speakers and keypad. The precisely fitted rear panel is also held in place by a large steel screw. A stainless steel grille protects the speaker from all too stormy expressions of enthusiasm; the speaker is also moisture-impregnated - this is not apparent at first glance, but can certainly become important in the heat of the game. The robustness of the entire construction means that Hörbert's child's foot can take it in its stride if it is accidentally knocked over - or if the fidgeting child's finger lays the device flat for quicker access. And even in the event of an unintentionally rough fall, Hörbert remains a faithful companion: all parts can be repaired or replaced.
Simply intuitive. Immediately understandable
A simple, intuitive operating concept, based on nine clearly arranged, colorful and robust wooden buttons, enables the device to be used immediately - your offspring will be able to "grasp" the operation quickly. The nine buttons can be used to access nine playlists; the child zaps through the respective playlist by repeatedly pressing the button. The black and gray buttons can be used to skip backwards and forwards within a song. It's child's play. As with the memory game, children will easily outperform their parents, parent friends and relatives when it comes to instantly finding their favorite song.
Playlists have never sounded better
Whether you use Bluetooth streaming, Internet radio via WLAN or the integrated memory card as a sound source: The songs and stories sound in amazingly good quality. The clean sound is particularly important to the manufacturer based at the foot of the Swabian Alb, because it is important to be able to hear "that it is called 'mustard' and not 'Sempf'". He is right: the development of expressiveness and vocabulary, a sense of rhythm and the art of singing goes hand in hand with a clear, pure sound. Hörbert offers high sound quality even at high volumes. In consideration of sensitive children's ears and adult nerves, the volume does not exceed 60 decibels in piano mode and a maximum of 70 decibels in forte mode - this is still below the maximum volume of 80 decibels specified by the EU safety standard for ear toys.

product_72.description:
General Information
Master of the Chair.
Hans J. Wegner (1914-2007) designed more than 500 chairs in his long professional life earning him the title “Master of the Chair”. Wegner is undisputedly the great figure of modern Scandinavian furniture design. Renowned Design museums like the MoMa in New York and the Neue Sammlung in Munich present complete series of his chairs. So much for the mark, he left in design history. His organically shaped, exquisite chairs, preferably made of light wood, set the tone in Scandinavian furniture design for decades; today, they enjoy almost archetypal status. Contemporary Scandinavian seating furniture seems to stem from these furnishing forefathers, although some of the children and children’s children bear a suspiciously strong resemblance to Wegner’s designs.
Wegner’s CH24 – The “Y-Chair”.
Admittedly, even the CH24 has ancestors. The chair is one of Wegner’s designs that owe their shape to his preoccupation with Chinese furniture construction. The seating furniture of the late Ming dynasty inspired him when he found the furnishings characterised by precisely what he tried to realise in his model chairs: a restrained-to-the-max design vocabulary and constructions that combine optimum stability with comfortable sitting. He took the basic idea of the Chinese Quanyi (internationally known as the “Horseshoe Chair”, recognisable by its strictly rectangular seat and its back and armrest curved like a horseshoe) and varied the design by inserting a filigree yet sufficiently stabilising Y-shaped element in place of the broad backrest-supporting backboard typical of the Quanyi. The CH24, however, is far more than a mere variation of a Chinese piece of furniture: To begin with, the construction of the substructure is unmistakably Scandinavian and lightweight. Furthermore, Wegner, who was always open to new, unusual materials, had the seat woven by hand from 120 metres of paper cord. The design of the CH24 dates back to 1949 and is by far Wegner’s most successful one. The chair, meanwhile well-known as the “Y-chair “or “Wishbone chair”, has been produced since 1950 – and still is – by Carl Hansen & Søn in Gelstedt near Odense. The Danes manufacture the classic chair – the process consists of more than 100 individual steps – in a number of pieces that keeps the price well below that of comparable style icons (and other Wegner models).
Light, strong and comfortable. Three classic chairs.
“A chair is a complicated object. Anyone who has ever tried to design a chair knows that. There are endless possibilities and many problems – a chair has to be lightweight, it has to be sturdy and comfortable at the same time. It is almost easier to build a skyscraper than a chair,” said Mies van der Rohe (1886-1969). As is well known, it did not stop him from designing chairs (and creating some classics in the process, most notably the Barcelona Chair in 1929). Nevertheless, his statement hits a nerve: the challenge he faced in the process is one that everyone is prone to discover who tries the same. And if, on top, a basic design idea – an aesthetic demand – goes into the mix, it becomes all the more complicated. Eventually, it is no surprise that the furniture market produces numerous “new” chairs year after year, but lasting classics are extremely rare among them.
We offer three models from a period that was very productive in this respect: the late 1940s and early 1950s. On the one hand, they represent (in the case of the “Y-Chair” or “Wishbone Chair” by the Dane Hans J. Wegner) the independent tradition of modern Scandinavian furniture design. On the other hand (in the case of Egon Eiermann’s chairs), they stand for the so-called “Second Modernism”. In post-war Germany, the design approach – and Egon Eiermann as a leading protagonist – successfully reclaimed the legacy of modern furniture design of the 1910s and 1920s Werkbund and Bauhaus design schools.

Weightless in space
The principle of the hammock - transferred to a simple piece of seating furniture. In its wide, fan-shaped hollow made of tightly woven fabric, the hanging chair supports the person sitting in it, floating in the room and thus enabling a relaxing, almost weightless sitting experience. It can be installed under the ceiling in the living room, but the hanging chair can also be used outdoors. The fabric is woven using a special endless weaving technique, in which a fixed number of continuous cotton threads are woven together in such a way that there are no annoying knots or loose edge threads in the fabric and each individual thread is firmly connected to the carrier rope. A fabric panel woven in this way is extremely tear-resistant and ensures an even load distribution; its material opulence can be felt at first touch. The wooden fixing rod prevents the mat from slipping together, while the swivel on the snap hook - both made of galvanized steel and therefore robust - allows the height of the hanging chair to be adjusted. All other work steps are carried out in the in-house twisting, weaving, carpentry and metal workshop - on partially self-developed and built milling and planing machines, glue presses and special looms.

What's more, it finds a (still) crumple-free zone in every room and can be quickly moved to wherever it is needed and wanted. This beanbag from the Senger manufactory tops the comfort with its quaint feathered creature design: the movable wings and legs as well as the long goose neck can be draped as desired and can therefore cuddle small and older children as cozily as a blanket (or a loving hug).
Natural materials and careful production by hand ensure that the feel-good and cuddly factor is long-lasting. The outer cover and ticking are made from pure organic cotton, while the filling for the head, neck and feet is made from pure new wool of German origin. The ticking of the (seat) torso is filled with spelt husks, which adapt comfortably to the body posture and, as a renewable raw material, are preferable to the commercially available, persistently squeaky plastic fillings made of polystyrene (Styrofoam). product_85.description:
General Information
Keep your posture casual. Exceptionally comfortable
It could hardly get any cozier: The seat of this bat chair, which curves in all directions, appears to be stretched out in space. You'll sit extremely comfortably in it and yet you won't lose your posture - not even when you sink back into the comfort of the Icelandic sheepskin.
Naturally cuddly. The Icelandic sheepskin
Icelandic sheep are extremely robust fellows who are perfectly at home even in the harsh Icelandic climate. They owe their "coolness" in the face of weather conditions above all to their unusually dense, long wool, which protects them from the cold and rain as well as the heat. Thanks to these natural air-conditioning properties of the Icelandic sheepskin, it is ideal for providing you with warming comfort in winter and a cozy comfort zone even in summer. The Mariposa armchair is made from vegetable-tanned Icelandic sheepskin whose wool has been shorn to a shorter length. The shearing makes the unbleached and undyed fur even more supple and easier to care for: you can easily vacuum it thoroughly for occasional cleaning (please set the vacuum cleaner to a low setting).
Filigree substructure. The frame
The Icelandic sheepskin is suspended in a frame made of powder-coated round steel rods (made in Sweden), which is supplied in individual parts and can be easily assembled into a whole using the enclosed die-cast aluminum connectors. In addition to the assembly instructions, each delivery contains fastening screws and a corresponding tool.
The butterfly. With all legs on the ground
In our opinion, this armchair, whose predecessor became famous as the "Butterfly Chair" (or bat chair) in the 1950s, is still one of the most successful pieces of seating furniture of its kind. The original was a simple armchair with a branched frame designed in the 1930s by Argentinian architects Antoni Bonet i Castellana, Juan Kurchan and Jorge Ferrari-Hardoy. The shape of our model is very similar to this original type and bears the name "Mariposa" - butterfly.

General Information
A chair as it is written in the book
And that nothing can knock over so quickly. Its frame is made of solid beech wood, the seat is available either as a seat frame with woven cane or as a plywood panel with upholstery and cowhide covering.
Rabenau. The chairmaking town
Rabenau's chairmaking tradition is almost 400 years old. The many special skills of Rabenau's chairmakers that have grown over that time have survived industrialization, and they have survived the Volkseigentum and the Federal Republic's Vocational Training Ordinance unscathed. Today, 16 factories work under the umbrella of a cooperative. They manufacture chairs and tables in a manner committed to the best traditions of the trade. What the Rabenauer chairmakers can do, they show especially in the faithful reproduction of historical models.
The Nikolai furniture
In 1910, the Rabenauer supplied the following seating furniture and tables to equip the four hundred year old "Old Nikolai School" at the Nikolaikirchhof in Leipzig. For the reopening of the renovated building as a cultural center in 1994, the furniture was built a second time in Rabenau. For "private use" they are only available from us.
The processing
The frames and seat frames of the Rabenau furniture are made of solid beech wood, which is stained and varnished. The wood joints are tapped and cold glued. The seat frames of the seating furniture are mitered and the edges are profile milled; typical leg shape with rod milling.
The seats: Leather or wicker
The seating surfaces are either leather seats or wickerwork:
- The leather seats consist of a plywood base, which is padded with upholstery wadding; black cowhide is fixed on it with decorative nails.
- For the wickerwork seating surfaces, the split, stained peddigree is woven three times by hand through holes in the chair fold.
Restoration possible

product_91.description:
General Information
As strong as an oak tree
By design, or even better, by workshop design, spindle stools are work furniture that fulfill a precisely defined purpose: to provide users with a flexible, adjustable seat height to give them an overview at work - at any table, for any height. The simple yet highly functional technical solution for this requirement is mechanical height adjustment via a threaded spindle. The formal design of such a stool also follows this purpose alone and is limited to the essentials: the frame inspired by the three-legged stool, a spindle, a seat - minimalism at its best. This example shows how the original workshop furniture can be transformed into an impressive, ultra-modern piece of home furniture with added interior design value: the spindle stool is made entirely from solid local oak, right down to its central element.
A spindle made of oak wood may come as a surprise at first, but oak wood is famous for being extremely hard, tough and durable. Even under water, it resists rotting for centuries. In short, not only many people and animals, but also this stool and its spindle are "strong as an oak", reliably lifting its user up and back down again and also conquering additional areas of use: Because thanks to the completely flat seat surface, it holds its own just as solidly as an adaptable side table. Whether you use it as a flexible seat or as a stable storage surface: The opulence of the material in the stool contrasts with the simplicity of the design in a visually exciting way, which fulfills its interior design function with lasting stability. Once you have chosen it, you won't be able to get rid of this spindle stool in a hurry. A handcrafted heirloom that moves between the poles of elegant restraint and strong character, proving its modernity over time.
Tradition x modernity. Mint Furniture
Anyone who still thinks that traditional craftsmanship results in furniture à la Gelsenkirchen Baroque should turn their gaze to Riga. There, the company Mint Furniture, founded in 2009, stands for furniture design in which the tried and tested is taken up and further developed in form and function. This is the essence of innovation anyway, especially when it wants to stand out from the mass of supposed modernity in a visionary way. The team at Mint Furniture, which combines knowledge of fine art, interior design, industrial design and craftsmanship, has also achieved something astonishing: an individual design signature that is revealed in the fine details. With his spindle stool made of solid oak, co-founder Janis Rauza laid the foundation for the creative combination of formal tradition and functional modernity. Continuously expanded, the entire furniture collection from Mint Furniture follows this vision: expertly crafted by cabinetmakers, supported by a profound knowledge of the possibilities of the material and supported by the use of modern technologies, the designs point far into the future as pieces for generations.

Coffee house chair No. 56 is manufactured in a factory founded by the sons and successors of Thonet in 1861 in the Moravian city of Bystritz am Hostein, today Bystrice pod Hostýnem in the Czech Republic. Despite the turns of fortune it is still known today as TON (továrny na ohýbaný nábytek – "Factory for Bentwood Furniture").Bystritz is thereby the oldest and most revered location in the world where furniture is still manufactured by manually bending wood.
Bent and embossed.
We offer the bentwood chairs with a black lacquered finish or in a stained und clear varnished brown. The chairs are embossed with the patterns from the old templates, a technique, which like the manufacture of the bentwood furniture itself, is an industrial procedure.
"Consumer furniture".
The selection of bentwood furniture TON manufactures is increasing annually, which one can see at the relevant furniture fairs every year. In addition the various chairs are still produced based on the earlier designs from the founding of the firm, which are considered classical chairs today. At the time those models which later became famous were mass produced (in the 19th century they were called "consumer furniture "). Which is how they became the coffee house chairs for an entire epoch. Chairs like those that became known as Model No. 14, with its curved backrest made of two bentwood arches, the coffee house chair par excellence, or the armchair No. 24, with its "palmette" executed backrest embodied designs which reflected the Zeitgeist. They owe their wide distribution to their minimal weight, their comfort and the fact because of their industrial manufacture, they were affordable, qualities which still distinguish them today.
Bent and embossed
We offer the bentwood chairs either black lacquered or braun stained and clear lacquered. Their seats are embossed with patterns based on old patterns - a technique that, like the manufacture of bentwood furniture itself, requires machine and industrial production.
"Consumer furniture"
The range of bentwood furniture that TON manufactures is wide - and year after year they are represented at the usual furniture fairs with novelties. In addition, the company produces a number of chairs that date back to the early designs of the Wilhelminian period and are considered classics today. First and foremost, however, even the later famous models were mass-produced items in their day (in the 19th century they spoke of "consumer furniture"). This was the only reason why they could become the typical coffee house chairs of an entire era. Chairs such as model No. 14 below with its curved backrest made of two bentwood arches - the coffee house chair par excellence - or the armrest chair No. 24 with its "palmette" backrest certainly met the taste of the time in terms of design. However, they owe their widespread popularity to their light weight, their indestructibility, their seating comfort and the fact that they were inexpensive as a result of industrial mass production - characteristics that distinguish them even today, above and beyond all design issues.
How the wood was bent
Revolutions in furniture making are a rather rare thing. The perfection of the bentwood chair by Michael Thonet (1796-1871) was such a revolutionary act - in three respects. From a technical point of view, the revolution had been in the offing since about 1830. Michael Thonet experimented with methods of making wood bendable under the effect of steam and glue water. He improved them step by step; in 1852, after several attempts, he finally obtained a patent that protected his method of "giving wood any bend and shape in various directions by cutting it up and gluing it back together." "Any bend" - this phrase hints at the second revolution. With the help of bentwood technology, it was also possible to break new ground in design; simple semicircular arches as backrests, round-shaped yet solid-wood combinations of chair backs and backrests, or even curved chair leg reinforcements were not only technical innovations, but also innovations in design. Thirdly, bentwood furniture marked an economic revolution. They were not only suitable for production on an industrial scale, they virtually required it. And so, even during Michael Thonet's lifetime, the idea of bentwood furniture led to an industry of its own. His sons and successors mass-produced bentwood chairs and founded numerous manufacturing plants, primarily in the Eastern European region, which at the time belonged to imperial and royal Austria. Austria, where labor was cheap and the supply of beech wood was almost inexhaustible. One of these factories was established in 1861 in the Moravian town of Bystritz am Hostein, now Bystrice pod Hostýnem in the Czech Republic. It operates after a checkered history as an independent joint stock company under the name TON (továrny na ohýbaný nábytek, in German "factory for bentwood furniture") still today: Bystritz is the oldest place in the world where furniture is made by bending wood by hand.

product_100.description:
General Information
Solid look. Solid workmanship
This stable, four-legged stool attracts attention for two reasons, but without pushing itself to the fore. Firstly, it impresses with a cushion-shaped seat that is completely flat on the surface, making it ideal for use as a side table. Secondly, the seat is made of six (!) centimetres thick Bavarian ash wood. This makes the seat material opulent and solid, but also visually remarkable, as the dark core typical of ash wood is not sorted out as usual, but is also used here. It is clearly visible in the seat and gives each chair an individual look. This also means that the stool delivered to your home will differ from the photo in terms of grain and color. Every stool looks a little different.
A gem made from solid wood
Auerberg in Bavaria manufactures the stool from local wood. The four oak legs are joined to the seat using the classic wedge-joint technique, or rather embedded in it, as can be seen from the circles in the seat. The choice of materials, design and the neat craftsmanship, including the joining technique and surface treatment, turn this inconspicuous piece of furniture into a solid wood gem that fits into any room in a timeless, classic manner.
Radically simple, completely functional: furniture from Auerberg
Radical reduction in form and material and a complete focus on function - that is the guiding principle behind the furniture from Auerberg. These are handcrafted products that are designed away from industrial standards, far removed from fashion and uninfluenced by marketing constraints and produced in small batches. Behind every single piece of furniture is the authentic personality of the respective designer - and because there is no restrictive program dictate, the product designers are only committed to their own standards. Accordingly, all Auerberg furniture is unmistakable, sometimes purist to the point of stubbornness, extremely solid in terms of craftsmanship and thus virtually made to last.
The furniture is manufactured regionally in Upper Bavaria and the wood - mostly oak, ash and beech - comes from certified forestry operations. The mastermind behind Auerberg is Christoph Böninger, once a professional globetrotter, now a settled design publisher. Well-connected in design circles, Böninger works in Munich and on his farm in Auerberg - hence the name of the project - near Bad Aibling. And even though Böninger has gathered a number of designers and architects around him for his "product lab" - with established greats standing alongside up-and-coming talent - he still lends a hand himself. Sometimes he oils wooden furniture and gets it ready for shipping. Incidentally, Auerberg's greatest successes to date include the AEKI step stool by Gerhardt Kellermann and the "Silent Ladder" by Christoph Böninger himself, a versatile hybrid of stepladder and silent servant.

product_101.description:
General Information
Always good for a surprise
There is room in even the smallest hut - but there is not necessarily enough seating available at all times. Elsewhere, they may be available, but it may be necessary to be able to easily move them aside to make room for dancing and merriment, for example. This poses a challenge for anyone who has more surprise guests than chairs and still wants to offer a comfortable place to sit down.
Whatever situation you find yourself in, the folding chair is the versatile, mobile and functional solution. It's there, it's gone, it's here, it's there - depending on your needs. And when it is as discreetly designed, sturdily made and comfortable to own as this folding chair, it is always good for a surprise and proves your hospitality as a fully-fledged seat. Just under six centimetres narrow when folded up, it completes your furnishings out of sight and waits inconspicuously for its use - where nothing can easily knock it out of shape, as it is made of solid oak. And fresh air lovers can rest assured: With the first ray of sunshine, it fulfills its task just as solidly and comfortably as a balcony and garden chair - the only thing you should always allow it is a covered storage space in rainy weather or when not in use.
Note:
Due to the high tannic acid content of oak wood, blue-black discoloration can occur on the wood surface in combination with moisture and in contact with ferrous metals. In addition, the so-called tannins can be washed out by rainwater and stain surfaces and adjacent materials.

The solid poplar bench board complements the CONTAINER DS KLEIN and the TARA KLEIN shelving unit and turns them into seating. The bench is supplied with attractive screws and the appropriate tools. Series Container DS
Synonymous with storage and transport: the container in its archetypal surface of folded steel. We offer this cabinet furniture in the miniaturized form of overseas containers in four different versions. These well-proportioned storage boxes serve many purposes and areas of use. All containers have perforations in the bottoms for passing cables. The classic container as well as the flat and small container have doors hinged to the top of the body, which slide into the top of the body when opened and thus almost completely disappear. The CONTAINER DS PLUS is upright and has a conventional hinged door on the side.
The classic: The CONTAINER DS in the proportion of a sea container is virtually the archetype of the series CONTAINER DS. It serves as a cabinet in the living room for china and utensils for the set table, in the office for storing files in standardized format or for paper and office utensils. As a chest of drawers for linen and as a piece of furniture in the hallway and wardrobe. It can be combined in its basic rectangular shape with a variety of complementary accessories. Various feet and casters or the two framework frames serve as the basis. The shelf element TARA has the outer contour of the container and can be stacked with it in height via connectors included in the delivery. The coat rack completes the container to a functional wardrobe. The container of this format is available in limited color selection equipped with a lock. It can be mounted on the wall with a separately available bracket.
The flat one: CONTAINER DS FLAT has the footprint of the classic CONTAINER DS and can be connected to it in height and stacked. It can be combined with the above mentioned accessories of the classic CONTAINER DS. This container often serves as a flat element that is built into a stack of the classic container. It is useful with its special volume for the stack of paper, for utensils and as a shelf for many purposes. It can be mounted on the wall with a separately available bracket.
The small one: The CONTAINER DS KLEIN as the little brother of the CONTAINER DS does not have the proportions of a sea container, unlike its archetypal big role model - it is narrower, with identical depth and height. With its small size and unusual formatting, it serves as a piece of side furniture next to the bed and sofa and can also be stacked up to form a tower. It can be equipped with all separate feet as well as the casters. Unlike its sister models, it is always equipped with a smooth cover shelf in the respective color. The shelf element TARA KLEIN has the outer contour of the container and can be stacked with it in height via connectors included in the delivery.
The big one: A very special piece of furniture with its own range of uses is the CONTAINER DS PLUS. This large container is stackable like all other sister models via included square connectors. product_115.description:
General Information
Tiger and friends in the living room.
You’ll form an attachment to these four-legged fellows, not because they are modest and easy to care for, or that in a pinch he could stand in as a pet. He’s also just so versatile, as a surface for a board game or a side table, as a stool or even a chest, with space in his belly to store books, stuffed animals and other toys. Or hide them ...
Werkhaus. Peg and Wedge Connectors 2.0.
The intelligent Werkhaus construction principle is astonishingly simple and needs no tools for assembly: The robust, shape-retaining HDF (high-density fiberboard) elements consist of panels made from fine wood fiber, glue and water. Precisely cut with CNC machines, the pieces fit together easily. You connect them by inserting a peg notched on both sides of one panel through a slot in a second panel. Then you fasten the peg with a rubber ring. The resulting lightweight units are astonishingly stable – despite relatively thin walls. While highly practical in use, they tolerate dismantling and reassembling at any time.
The reversible connection technology, the choice of materials and the machine manufacturing process allow for the construction of complex, at the same time very inexpensive products predestined for sales displays in stores and trade fairs. Unsurprisingly, this kind of furniture rapidly became the main business of the 1992 founded firm.
Lots of Drawers. Ready with Little Effort.
Thanks to the precise cutting and the clean machine processing, the affordable furnishings can be constructed from only 3 to 6 mm thin boards. Such furniture would be much more difficult and therefore much more expensive to produce by carpenters. Besides, the visible plug-in connections of peg, wedge and rubber rings create a unique design language, particularly evident in the monochrome versions. Werkhaus develops and manufactures all its products at its headquarters in Lower Saxony. We deliver individual parts; however, we are sure you’ll find the assembling an easy undertaking.

product_116.description:
General Information
Bent and embossed
We offer the bentwood chairs either black lacquered or braun stained and clear lacquered. Their seats are embossed with patterns based on old patterns - a technique that, like the manufacture of bentwood furniture itself, requires machine and industrial production.
"Consumer furniture"
The range of bentwood furniture that TON manufactures is wide - and year after year they are represented at the usual furniture fairs with novelties. In addition, the company produces a number of chairs that date back to the early designs of the Wilhelminian period and are considered classics today. First and foremost, however, even the later famous models were mass-produced items in their day (in the 19th century they spoke of "consumer furniture"). This was the only reason why they could become the typical coffee house chairs of an entire era. Chairs such as model No. 14 below with its curved backrest made of two bentwood arches - the coffee house chair par excellence - or the armrest chair No. 24 with its "palmette" backrest certainly met the taste of the time in terms of design. However, they owe their widespread popularity to their light weight, their indestructibility, their seating comfort and the fact that they were inexpensive as a result of industrial mass production - characteristics that distinguish them even today, above and beyond all design issues.
How the wood was bent
Revolutions in furniture making are a rather rare thing. The perfection of the bentwood chair by Michael Thonet (1796-1871) was such a revolutionary act - in three respects. From a technical point of view, the revolution had been in the offing since about 1830. Michael Thonet experimented with methods of making wood bendable under the effect of steam and glue water. He improved them step by step; in 1852, after several attempts, he finally obtained a patent that protected his method of "giving wood any bend and shape in various directions by cutting it up and gluing it back together." "Any bend" - this phrase hints at the second revolution. With the help of bentwood technology, it was also possible to break new ground in design; simple semicircular arches as backrests, round-shaped yet solid-wood combinations of chair backs and backrests, or even curved chair leg reinforcements were not only technical innovations, but also innovations in design. Thirdly, bentwood furniture marked an economic revolution. They were not only suitable for production on an industrial scale, they virtually required it. And so, even during Michael Thonet's lifetime, the idea of bentwood furniture led to an industry of its own. His sons and successors mass-produced bentwood chairs and founded numerous manufacturing plants, primarily in the Eastern European region, which at the time belonged to imperial and royal Austria. Austria, where labor was cheap and the supply of beech wood was almost inexhaustible. One of these factories was established in 1861 in the Moravian town of Bystritz am Hostein, now Bystrice pod Hostýnem in the Czech Republic. It operates after a checkered history as an independent joint stock company under the name TON (továrny na ohýbaný nábytek, in German "factory for bentwood furniture") still today: Bystritz is the oldest place in the world where furniture is made by bending wood by hand.

product_117.description:
General Information
A chair as it is written in the book
And that nothing can knock over so quickly. Its frame is made of solid beech wood, the seat is available either as a seat frame with woven cane or as a plywood panel with upholstery and cowhide covering.
Rabenau. The chairmaking town
Rabenau's chairmaking tradition is almost 400 years old. The many special skills of Rabenau's chairmakers that have grown over that time have survived industrialization, and they have survived the Volkseigentum and the Federal Republic's Vocational Training Ordinance unscathed. Today, 16 factories work under the umbrella of a cooperative. They manufacture chairs and tables in a manner committed to the best traditions of the trade. What the Rabenauer chairmakers can do, they show especially in the faithful reproduction of historical models.
The Nikolai furniture
In 1910, the Rabenauer supplied the following seating furniture and tables to equip the four hundred year old "Old Nikolai School" at the Nikolaikirchhof in Leipzig. For the reopening of the renovated building as a cultural center in 1994, the furniture was built a second time in Rabenau. For "private use" they are only available from us.
The processing
The frames and seat frames of the Rabenau furniture are made of solid beech wood, which is stained and varnished. The wood joints are tapped and cold glued. The seat frames of the seating furniture are mitered and the edges are profile milled; typical leg shape with rod milling.
The seats: Leather or wicker
The seating surfaces are either leather seats or wickerwork:
- The leather seats consist of a plywood base, which is padded with upholstery wadding; black cowhide is fixed on it with decorative nails.
- For the wickerwork seating surfaces, the split, stained peddigree is woven three times by hand through holes in the chair fold.
Restoration possible
In cooperation with the Rabenau chair makers, we offer to refurbish older models of chairs of this type. You will receive an offer on request, the duration of the restoration depends on the effort.

product_118.product_name: Stand spotlight Wittenberg, Deep black RAL 9005
product_118.alt_text: Stand spotlight Wittenberg, Deep black RAL 9005
product_118.description:
General Information
In this model, the ceiling- and wall-mounted spotlight WITTENBERG becomes a luminaire that you can position on any ground. The spotlight type DRUFF performs its service wherever you need accent lighting from below or when there is no power supply via wall or ceiling outlets. DRUFF may stand on the floor, on top of a sideboard, or a shelf. WITTENBERG 4.0 features an intricate, beautifully crafted housing that dispenses with visible screws or cables. The spotlight heads sit slightly recessed in the rectangular housing; nevertheless, you can rotate them 365 degrees and tilt them 90 degrees. When maintenance tasks are required, a patented bayonet catch enables you to detach the entire light head from the housing in the blink of an eye. The light emission angle of the lamps is 12 degrees, providing focused light. We have two attachment lenses included in the delivery. These lenses create a light output of 38 degrees and give off a wide beam. Cable: L 250 cm, safety plug (type F). The luminaire contains LED lamps. Luminous flux: 1,100 lm, colour temperature: 2,700 K, colour rendering index (CRI > 90), wattage rating: 2 × 12.7 W. Swappable optics: beam angle 12° and 38°.
wittenberg 4.0 - the all-rounder
The variety and flexibility of the wittenberg system luminaire family is unsurpassed. wittenberg 4.0 is the most versatile system luminaire from mawa and is very often used in customized applications. With the fourth generation of the multifunctional light head, the entire luminaire series has been technically enhanced and formally reduced to what is possible. Future compatibility and a conscious use of resources are particularly important to mawa.
mawa
The brand identity of mawa, the luminaire manufacturer based on the outskirts of Berlin, comprises producing luminaires and lighting systems with innovative technologies and resourceful manufacturing processes. Designs that promise longevity are the main focus of mawa’s development and design department. One of the manufacturer’s primary concerns is to keep the consumption of resources in the production of luminaires in balance. From the first sketches to the prototypes ready for series production, luminaires by mawa are unique originals. Awarded with many design prizes, they grace museum collections all over the world. The brand’s small crew – with lighting enthusiast, founder, and doyen Martin Wallroth at the centre – has been a force to be reckoned with in the industry for years. They excelled in luminaire development (as represented in our range) as well as in lighting design for exhibitions, museums and trade fair stands. In all areas, mawa products are convincing in terms of design, material, finish, details, and lighting technology.

product_122.product_name: Tonone floor lamp steel and aluminum, White
product_122.alt_text: Tonone floor lamp steel and aluminum, White
product_122.description:
General Information
Outstanding Industrial Design.
The clever concept for this modular luminaire series comes from the Netherlands. The creative mind behind it is Anton de Groof, neither designer nor engineer, but enthusiastic about traditional mechanics and technology. Accordingly, the design language of the luminaires reminds us of mechanical constructions. It does justice to the industrial manufacturing process and combines simplicity with a well-thought-out way to guide the light. Each one a simple beauty, one may think of the Bauhaus school when looking at the design of these lamps.
Tonone luminaires. Exemplary industrial design
The clever modular concept for Tonone luminaires comes from the Netherlands. The designing mind behind it is Anton de Groof, who is neither a designer nor an engineer, but enthusiastic about traditional mechanics and technology. Consequently, the design language of the lamps is that of a mechanical construction that does justice to the industrial manufacturing process and combines simplicity with spirit in a thoughtful way - which places them formally in the environment of Bauhaus and Werkbund. It is noteworthy that the lights are not only mature, but also economically keep the all too rarely realized promise of industrial design to deliver technically as well as aesthetically high quality products at affordable prices.
All models in the series are built from always recurring identical parts. This starts with the heavy cast iron base, made in Belgium, and extends to the steel arm segments, which, like the aluminum shade, are covered with a highly reflective powder coating. Each joint is multiply adjustable thanks to five steel balls between two perforated discs with 23 holes - but only at angles that won't pinch your fingers or cause the lamp to tip. The enclosed adjustment key is reminiscent of old industrial luminaires. Tonone luminaires are switched by a push switch located just outside the shade on the socket. The lampshades are open at the top and bottom, which allows them to shine downward light on a surface to be illuminated and upward to contribute to indirect room lighting.
Purist. The Bolt series
Puristic, clear and functional are the lights of the series Bolt. All models consist of recurring, identical parts. This begins with the heavy cast iron base, manufactured in Belgium, and extends to the steel arm segments, which, like the aluminum lampshade, are covered with a highly reflective powder coating. Each joint is multiply adjustable thanks to five steel balls between two perforated discs with 23 holes - but only at angles that won't pinch your fingers or cause the lamp to tip. The included adjustment key is reminiscent of old industrial luminaires. The lampshades are open at the top and bottom, so they cast downward light onto the surface to be illuminated and contribute upward to indirect room lighting. The Bolt series is switched by a push switch located just outside the shade on the socket.

Wood and Glass. The Cesta.
Cesta (basket) is the name of this versatile lamp. You find its origin neither in Japan nor Scandinavia but in Barcelona. It is a stroke of luck that Santa & Cole, in collaboration with Milá, gave the Cesta an evolutionary boost before reissuing it. The original rattan frame is now made of steam-bent cherry wood, and the shade – still featuring circular cut-outs at the top and bottom – is made of single-layer etched glass instead of plastic. The swivelling handle makes it easy to move the lamp from A to B – from table to floor, for example. You can even use it on balconies and terraces as long as the weather is dry. In any case, thanks to its dimmer switch, it provides a soft to veritable, perfectly homogeneous and glare-free light.

product_131.description:
General Information
The Schliephacke. Floor, table and bed lamp in one
In the rooms of the student union Eichkamp in Berlin-Grunewald, this lamp was originally intended to provide light. Because in this form of housing the spatial conditions were (and are) known to be cramped, its designer Fridtjof Schliephacke created in 1959 a form that can be used either as a table lamp, floor lamp or bed lamp and can provide both direct and indirect light.
The basic structure of the lamp is - as is common with bauhaus close Objekten - constructed for industrial production. On the base in the form of a cast iron plate stand two aluminum spars, which are connected by bolts in three heights. The arm of the luminaire can stand upright between the uprights or be hooked into the aluminum uprights by means of milled grooves at the three heights of the bolts - at right angles to them or in a variable inclined position. The uppermost part of the arm can be locked in any position with a wing screw, and the reflector can be rotated through 360°.
Even though the manufacture of the lamp proved in the end far too expensive to equip entire dormitories with it, the moderately affectionately dubbed "Berlin frying pan" found its way into the homes of quite a few people interested in design.
Lighting for Living Areas and Museum Exhibitions. Mawa Design.
Mawa Design was founded in 1977 by Martin Wallroth in Berlin-Kreuzberg. Wallroth initially developed and produced objects for the living area and often played a pioneering role for formative ideas in product design. In the 1980s, he began fruitful collaborations with external designers excelling at bringing product ideas quickly to commercial viability thanks to the company’s flexible structure. While diligently producing the various serial models, Mawa customized a selection of products to different specifications: Luminaires for the master houses at the Bauhaus Dessau, the home of Corbusier, the University of the Arts and the Maxim Gorki Theatre in Berlin, the Treptow Crematorium and the Luther House in Wittenberg were among them. And last but not least, museums worldwide present Mawa luminaires, renowned for high-quality materials and unsurpassed technical implementation, as parts of their collections.
Combining Manufacture Skills and High-Technology Knowledge.
Mawa luminaires have always been at the cutting edge of light design while excelling at the technical execution and directing the light with regard to the fancied visual impact. Groundbreaking innovations in the lighting sector, such as the LED filament light bulbs, immediately found their way into the Mawa product cosmos. A decisive factor in the entrepreneurial success of Mawa Design was (and still is) the extraordinary combination of design studio and manufactory. Since 1997, the company has been based in the Palmhof, a renovated and listed historical monument in Langerwisch near Potsdam. Eventually, the manufactory offers enough space for all employees and the creation and production of the numerous in-house designs such as the wall and mirror lamp “Linestra”, the wall and ceiling lamps “Etna” and “Eintopf”, plus lighting classics of other renowned designers such as the pendant lamp “Havanna” designed by Wilhelm Braun-Feldweg or the floor lamp “Schliephacke” named after its creator.

product_132.description:
General Information
Stable light giver
In the porcelain base of this floor lamp hides a solid steel weight, which gives it a decent stability. To protect the floor, it is equipped with a felt base. The lampshade made of bone china, at an exposed height, perfectly shows off the light-technical advantages of the material. The lamp is switched by means of a foot switch on the power cable.
Translucent Porcelain. Bone China
"Bone China" or "bone china" is one of the finest porcelains. It is bright white and highly resistant to breakage even when drawn out wafer-thin. The most surprising property of bone china, however, is its translucency, silky shimmer and warm hue. The secret of the production of bone china, long known only in China, was revealed around the middle of the 18th century by a small earthenware factory in England: By adding bone ash, it was possible to fire translucent porcelain in a stoneware kiln at 1,200°C. Even today, the difficult mixture of kaolin, feldspar, silica sand and more than 50% vitrified bone ash limits the mechanization of manufacturing and worldwide the number of manufactories that master this craft.
British, in Detail. Lamps from BTC.
Lamps made by BTC (= British Timeless Classics), in the vicinity of Oxford, have attained the status of timeless classics. The creative spirit and driving force behind the firm is Peter Bowles, who pursues his very clear idea and just as clearly realises his agenda. The process starts with the manufacture: Bowles wants to produce lamps that are British down to the level of detail. For example, the bone china-lamp shades come from a pottery in Stoke-on-Trent, known as the "the Potteries" because of the almost 500 potteries that used to be located there. Almost all are gone today and the firm, which also belongs to Bowles, would not exist except for BTC. He took it over when it was on the brink of bankruptcy and has restructured it while keeping all the employees. The hand-blown glass domes come from a glass blowing shop in Worcestershire which Bowles also bought. In addition to domes for lamps, the shop produces coloured glass windows for historical buildings and churches. A handful of glass blowers with their two small smelting furnaces practice the methods of glass blowing and uphold the once famous English tradition of this trade. The British manufacture of the lamps extends to the cables, too. Bowles was dissatisfied with the plastic wrapped cables on his first lamp, so he used a locally produced cloth wrapped cable from a clothes iron for his exhibition piece. The reaction was so positive that he has used cloth cable since. They are locally produced near the firm in home-based work.

General Information
Sadhana: Sage, palo santo, papyrus and frankincense provide a subtle, warm-spicy, slightly sweet fragrance that is particularly pleasant during meditation.
Natural fragrance. Harmonizing effect
The candles contain pure natural essential oils whose soothing fragrance harmonizes your meditation and yoga practice. As with the perfumes from Aimée de Mars, these fragrance compositions are also based on aromatherapeutic findings in order to facilitate a comprehensive sense of well-being. You can use the yoga and meditation candles to create a calming and harmonizing atmosphere in your home, making it easier for you to let go of the stress of the day. The essential oils also have a "purifying" effect on the air in the room.
The wax is purely plant-based and is made from soy and coconut oil.
Aimée de Mars. Fragrances from the Aroma Perfumery.
The Parisian perfume house Aimée de Mars has dedicated itself to natural fragrances resulting in the commitment that the fragrances’ ingredients are of natural origin. The perfumes consist of 95% natural ingredients and thus meet the requirements of natural cosmetics, although Aimée de Mars has deliberately refrained from certification. product_148.description:
General Information
The fresh, woody-resinous notes of Japanese cypress help to calm and clear the mind.
Fragrance at a stroke. Incense sticks to go
They look like matches and are just as easy to use. However, the scented matches do not burn, but smoulder after lighting and then release their pleasant aroma for ten minutes. All you need is a fireproof base on which to place them - which is included in every pack. This means you can use the incense sticks anytime, anywhere and on any day and take a short break. This is also where the name of the incense matches comes from: Hibi means "day for day" or "daily" in Japanese. The small incense sticks are made of washi, not wood like conventional matches. They get most of their aroma from vegetable oils and raw materials, including frankincense, to which they owe their high quality. Some fragrances have to be produced synthetically so that the composition is heat-resistant. The aromas range from classic to originally Japanese, such as the yuzu scent or Japanese cypress.
Synthesis of two traditional products
The idea for these ingenious scented matches came from a Japanese match manufacturer. The search for a second mainstay - because the use of matches has been steadily declining for years and because he himself is an ardent fan of incense - gave him the idea of developing incense sticks in a miniature format. The right partner for this project was right on his doorstep, as the company's site in Hyogo Prefecture not only has a long tradition of producing matches, but also incense sticks. In 2011, Kobe Match (which has been manufacturing matches since 1929) and the Daihatsu incense factory, which was founded in 1897, began joint development work and launched the small, fragrant sticks onto the market three years later. Incidentally, the logo takes up the aspect of daily incense burning: It shows the Chinese character 日 for day twice.
Hint:
Don’t leave this item unattended when using it. During use, please place it on a fireproof base.

product_152.product_name: Coudre Berlin scented candle, Rosemary & Lavender
product_152.alt_text: Coudre Berlin scented candle, Rosemary & Lavender
product_152.description:
General Information
Good Things Will Happen Soon
This candle aims to inspire a confident view of the world: The spicy floral scent of lavender is harmoniously complemented by the fresh herbal notes and woody-tart undertones of rosemary.
Coudre Berlin. From a single mold
"Coudre" means "to sew". When it comes to scented candles, the name of the Berlin label may be confusing, but before the scented candles came fashion, or more precisely: a new menswear collection. It all began in 2016, when Berliners Dimitri Moustakidis and Daniel Diederich had just launched their first collection of timeless basics and were now looking for ways to add an atmospheric touch to their creations. After all, fashion is not just a piece of fabric on the body; clothing also reflects a mood. Fashion and mood from a single source: the two designers finally decided on candles that would capture an atmosphere olfactorily and inspire at the same time. Moustakidis and Diederich developed their first fragrance compositions in a small kitchen in Prenzlauer Berg - with the aim of using only natural raw materials and ingredients. Once they had found a scent that appealed to them, they captured it in the candles - and poured each individual candle by hand.
Little by little, a whole series of scented candles was created. Despite the success of their creations and compositions, Coudre Berlin continues to attach great importance to meticulous craftsmanship. Each scented candle is still poured by hand in a Berlin workshop and only natural ingredients are used. The vegetable wax is made from sunflower and olive oil, while the olfactory ingredient is pure essential oils. Practical additional benefit: The scented candles are poured into brewing jars with Bakelite® screw-on lids. Once all wax residue has been removed and thoroughly cleaned, the jars can be reused as storage containers.
Note:
When burning the candle for the first time, please allow it to burn until the entire surface has liquefied. Only then will the fragrance molecules dissolve completely and the fragrance can unfold optimally. This also prevents a funnel and ultimately a tunnel from forming in the wax. To extinguish the flame, simply dip the wick briefly into the wax with a match and put it back in place. This prevents soot from forming and the candle burns well again. The next time you light the candle, make sure that the wick is not too long; it is best to shorten it regularly to 0.5 centimeters. Wax residue on the glass wall can be liquefied by briefly placing the glass in the oven at 60 °C. If you wish to continue using the jar, please remove any wax residue and clean the jar with hot water and washing-up liquid.
Warnings
Attention
H317: May cause allergic skin reactions.
H412: Harmful to aquatic organisms, with long lasting effects.
P101: If medical advice is required, have packaging or label ready.
P102: Keep out of the reach of children.
P273: Avoid release into the environment.
P280: Wear protective gloves/protective clothing/eye protection/face protection.
P333 + P313: In case of skin irritation or rash: Seek medical advice/attention.
P501: Dispose of contents/container in accordance with national regulations.

product_155.product_name: Looops scented candle with wooden lid, Mountain air
product_155.alt_text: Looops scented candle with wooden lid, Mountain air
product_155.description:
General Information
Mountain air: forest-fresh scent of Swiss stone pine needles, juniper branches and lemon peel, reminiscent of a hike in the mountains. Aromatherapy effect: helps to clear the head, strengthen and balance.
Nature in a candle. Smells good and does you good
Bring the scent of nature indoors? These candles can do just that: whether spicy forest air with a tangy Swiss stone pine aroma (mountain air), spicy lavender scent with juniper (leisure time) or rosemary notes (homecoming) or fruity orange and lemon notes with warm cinnamon and vanilla aromas (evening gold). Many find the fragrances soothingly relaxing or pleasantly invigorating, depending on the aroma. In these candles, the well-composed blends of exclusively natural essential plant oils provide the intense fragrance. The candle wax is also obtained from purely plant-based raw materials (from rapeseed and soy) - so you can breathe deeply and relax twice as much. And for a long time, because the vegetable wax burns significantly longer than mineral oil-based wax. Once the scented candle has burned down, you can use the decorative jar for a variety of purposes, as it comes with a lid made from certified, dark-stained oak wood. Another practical feature is that it can be used as a saucer for the burning scented candle, protecting the base from heat. Half of the smoked glass is made from recycled glass.
Looops has given its scented candles a new look and, in some cases, a new name. If you are already familiar with the candles and would now like to buy the fireplace whisper, choose the Homecoming scented candle, the feel-good time has turned into leisure time.
Capture fragrances. Bringing nature home
In the mountains, they say, the mind is free. It was in the mountains, more precisely in the Salzkammergut on the northern edge of the Alps, that Julia Schliefsteiner and Markus Niederfriniger came up with the idea of their own fragrancekerzen-Manufaktur to capture and preserve the scents of nature and take them home with them. The fire was lit: they founded Looops Kerzenmanuaktur, and the deeper they delved into the world of fragrances and aromas, the more they realized how far-reaching their effects could be and that the findings of aromatherapy could be wonderfully combined with their new craft. So Julia Schliefsteiner went straight on to complete her aromatherapy training and is now very familiar with the gentle extraction of essential oils and their effects.
Nature as inspiration and source
True to their principle "Nature is good the way it is", they add neither artificial nor synthetic substances and use vegetable wax obtained from rapidly renewable plants (soy and rapeseed) - which also has the advantage that these plant-based candles burn longer and produce less soot than mineral oil-based ones. The wicks are made of pure cotton or even wood. Julia Schliefsteiner creates all the fragrances herself in the company's own "kitchen" near Salzburg. The scented candles are also made by hand there - a complex process involving many steps. It begins with the extraction of the valuable, fragrant and highly effective oils from herbs, flowers and fruits. For new creations, the mixtures of essential oils are first left to rest for a while so that the various fragrance components can blend into a single unit. Only then are small test candles poured and the fragrances tested over several days. The creations are usually inspired by the landscape of the Salzkammergut, the herbs on the mountain pasture or the forest shortly after the rain. After all, a hike through the mountains and nature not only clears the mind, but also fills it with new ideas.
Note:
When burning the candle for the first time, please allow it to burn until the entire surface has liquefied. Only then will the fragrance molecules dissolve completely and the fragrance can unfold optimally. This also prevents a funnel and ultimately a tunnel from forming in the wax. To extinguish the flame, simply dip the wick briefly into the wax with a match and put it back in place. This prevents soot from forming and the candle burns well again. The next time you light the candle, make sure that the wick is not too long; it is best to shorten it regularly to 0.5 centimeters. Wax residue on the glass wall can be liquefied by briefly placing the glass in the oven at 60 °C. If you wish to continue using the jar, please remove any wax residue and clean the jar with hot water and washing-up liquid.

Warnings
EUH208: Contains limonene. May cause allergic reactions.

The scent of cotton blossom, cherry blossom and wild cedar.
Natural essences and essential oils give these scented candles their clearly perceptible, yet distinctly pleasant subtle fragrance. Powdery, with a hint of fruity or woody nunacs, they exude their delicate aroma for up to 50 hours. The basis is pure vegetable wax, made from soybean and sunflower oil. Three scents are available: powdery cotton blossom, subtle fruity cherry blossom or wild cedar with woody notes.

The scents are fresh creations of uncomplicated and light character, made from natural extracts and essential oils sourced from the region. The formulations come from Perfumers in Grasse, and Panier des Sens produces its scents in the tradition-steeped town near the French Riviera according to the classical artistry of perfumery.

product_161.product_name: Rape candle Weck® jar, Verbena Mint
product_161.alt_text: Rape candle Weck® jar, Verbena Mint
product_161.description:
General Information
Rediscovered crop. Rapeseed
If you travel to Schleswig-Holstein in April and May, you will pass many yellow rapeseed fields, which set the wide, hilly landscape in a particularly beautiful light. Rapeseed has always been one of the most important sources of oil here, but is also important for crop rotation in agriculture, partly because it can break chains of infection in cereal diseases. While rapeseed oil was primarily used for lamp oil or lubricating oil for industry and soap production until the middle of the 19th century, it was soon replaced by cheap petroleum-based fuels and edible oils from overseas. It is only since the 1970s that rapeseed oil can also be used as cooking oil and animal feed, thanks to new varieties that contain almost no bitter erucic acid. Since then, the area under cultivation has been steadily increasing and the possible uses have also been further developed.
Fragrant rapeseed candles
The Itzehoer candle manufacturer produces these scented candles on the basis of rapeseed oil. This not only has the advantage of being a regional, renewable raw material that can be procured via short transportation routes, but the candles are also purely plant-based and completely free of harmful substances. Rapeseed wax is also very suitable as a carrier for scented oils, which are initially safely enclosed in the wax and only develop their full aroma when the candle burns. In this case, it is pure essential oils that give the candles their pleasant fragrance. They come with a candle holder in the shape of a classic Weck® jar with a lid - and are therefore ready for immediate use.

product_164.description:
General Information
Fine accent. Subtle fragrance
The classic beehive, also known by beekeepers as a "hive" or "inverted hive", is a development of humans, not honey bees. Wild bees do not need such dwellings; most species do not even form colonies, but live solitary lives. They colonize cavities in the ground or in walls and rocks, between dead wood or in stems, tree trunks and the like. However, the hive of a honey bee colony cared for by a beekeeper has become so engrained in the collective imagination that the beehive is inevitably associated with every bee colony collecting nectar and pollen.
The beehive candle is an aesthetic reminiscence of the honey bee and its industrious service to mankind. Hand-cast in a North German candle manufactory, this "hive" also exudes the subtle scent of summer blossom and honey as a purely decorative element and adds a subtle accent to your creative interior design. When you light the candle, it spreads its warm light for many hours. (If, on the other hand, you are - at least inwardly - in favor of a fireless arrangement with some bees: You can also find these in our range, felted by hand from pure new wool and as durable as the unlit candle).
Note:
