product_165.product_name: Looops scented candle with wooden lid, Leisure time
product_165.alt_text: Looops scented candle with wooden lid, Leisure time
product_165.description:
General Information
Leisure time: with the floral and spicy scent of lavender, whose balancing and calming effect many appreciate from time immemorial, and juniper berry scent. Aromatherapy effect: supports relaxation and stress relief.
Nature in a candle. Smells good and does you good
Bring the scent of nature indoors? These candles can do just that: whether spicy forest air with a tangy Swiss stone pine aroma (mountain air), spicy lavender scent with juniper (leisure time) or rosemary notes (homecoming) or fruity orange and lemon notes with warm cinnamon and vanilla aromas (evening gold). Many find the fragrances soothingly relaxing or pleasantly invigorating, depending on the aroma. In these candles, the well-composed blends of exclusively natural essential plant oils provide the intense fragrance. The candle wax is also obtained from purely plant-based raw materials (from rapeseed and soy) - so you can breathe deeply and relax twice as much. And for a long time, because the vegetable wax burns significantly longer than mineral oil-based wax. Once the scented candle has burned down, you can use the decorative jar for a variety of purposes, as it comes with a lid made from certified, dark-stained oak wood. Another practical feature is that it can be used as a saucer for the burning scented candle, protecting the base from heat. Half of the smoked glass is made from recycled glass.
Looops has given its scented candles a new look and, in some cases, a new name. If you are already familiar with the candles and would now like to buy the fireplace whisper, choose the Homecoming scented candle, the feel-good time has turned into leisure time.
Capture fragrances. Bringing nature home
In the mountains, they say, the mind is free. It was in the mountains, more precisely in the Salzkammergut on the northern edge of the Alps, that Julia Schliefsteiner and Markus Niederfriniger came up with the idea of their own fragrancekerzen-Manufaktur to capture and preserve the scents of nature and take them home with them. The fire was lit: they founded Looops Kerzenmanuaktur, and the deeper they delved into the world of fragrances and aromas, the more they realized how far-reaching their effects could be and that the findings of aromatherapy could be wonderfully combined with their new craft. So Julia Schliefsteiner went straight on to complete her aromatherapy training and is now very familiar with the gentle extraction of essential oils and their effects.
Nature as inspiration and source
True to their principle "Nature is good the way it is", they add neither artificial nor synthetic substances and use vegetable wax obtained from rapidly renewable plants (soy and rapeseed) - which also has the advantage that these plant-based candles burn longer and produce less soot than mineral oil-based ones. The wicks are made of pure cotton or even wood. Julia Schliefsteiner creates all the fragrances herself in the company's own "kitchen" near Salzburg. The scented candles are also made by hand there - a complex process involving many steps. It begins with the extraction of the valuable, fragrant and highly effective oils from herbs, flowers and fruits. For new creations, the mixtures of essential oils are first left to rest for a while so that the various fragrance components can blend into a single unit. Only then are small test candles poured and the fragrances tested over several days. The creations are usually inspired by the landscape of the Salzkammergut, the herbs on the mountain pasture or the forest shortly after the rain. After all, a hike through the mountains and nature not only clears the mind, but also fills it with new ideas.
Note:
When burning the candle for the first time, please allow it to burn until the entire surface has liquefied. Only then will the fragrance molecules dissolve completely and the fragrance can unfold optimally. This also prevents a funnel and ultimately a tunnel from forming in the wax. To extinguish the flame, simply dip the wick briefly into the wax with a match and put it back in place. This prevents soot from forming and the candle burns well again. The next time you light the candle, make sure that the wick is not too long; it is best to shorten it regularly to 0.5 centimeters. Wax residue on the glass wall can be liquefied by briefly placing the glass in the oven at 60 °C. If you wish to continue using the jar, please remove any wax residue and clean the jar with hot water and washing-up liquid.

product_172.product_name: Looops refill scented candle, Mountain air
product_172.alt_text: Looops refill scented candle, Mountain air
product_172.description:
General Information
Mountain air: forest-fresh scent of Swiss stone pine needles, juniper branches and lemon peel, reminiscent of a hike in the mountains. Aromatherapy effect: helps to clear the head, strengthen and balance.
Looops scented candles for refilling
Looops has developed the scented candles in this format with paper cup especially for refilling the jars with wooden lids. This means you can use the jars for a long time. As the wax is purely vegetable, it can be easily washed off the jars with hot water and a little washing-up liquid. Please note that the candles must not be lit in the paper cup, as it is not fireproof and does not stand securely. To make it easier to remove the candles, place the cup in the freezer for about an hour: the wax will then separate better from the cup wall. The four fragrances available are Mountain Air, Leisure Time, Homecoming and Evening Gold.
Capture fragrances. Bringing nature home
In the mountains, they say, the mind is free. It was in the mountains, more precisely in the Salzkammergut on the northern edge of the Alps, that Julia Schliefsteiner and Markus Niederfriniger came up with the idea of their own fragrancekerzen-Manufaktur to capture and preserve the scents of nature and take them home with them. The fire was lit: they founded Looops Kerzenmanuaktur, and the deeper they delved into the world of fragrances and aromas, the more they realized how far-reaching their effects could be and that the findings of aromatherapy could be wonderfully combined with their new craft. So Julia Schliefsteiner went straight on to complete her aromatherapy training and is now very familiar with the gentle extraction of essential oils and their effects.
Nature as inspiration and source
True to their principle "Nature is good the way it is", they add neither artificial nor synthetic substances and use vegetable wax obtained from rapidly renewable plants (soy and rapeseed) - which also has the advantage that these plant-based candles burn longer and produce less soot than mineral oil-based ones. The wicks are made of pure cotton or even wood. Julia Schliefsteiner creates all the fragrances herself in the company's own "kitchen" near Salzburg. The scented candles are also made by hand there - a complex process involving many steps. It begins with the extraction of the valuable, fragrant and highly effective oils from herbs, flowers and fruits. For new creations, the mixtures of essential oils are first left to rest for a while so that the various fragrance components can blend into a single unit. Only then are small test candles poured and the fragrances tested over several days. The creations are usually inspired by the landscape of the Salzkammergut, the herbs on the mountain pasture or the forest shortly after the rain. After all, a hike through the mountains and nature not only clears the mind, but also fills it with new ideas.

product_175.description:
General Information
Night lamp for bright, flicker-free lighting.
For its size, this handy night lamp gives off a surprisingly bright, flicker-free light. It also takes up little space and can be easily carried to wherever it is needed using the curved handle.
More Light, No Soot. Karlskrona Paraffin Lamps.
In the evolution of non-electric sources of light, lamps burning paraffin oil have always played an important role – particularly those with a round wick and a centre draught burner. These burners are equipped with a flat, wide wick which not only links the reservoir with the burner but forms a circle in the burner unit and therefore gives off far more light than an ordinary flat wick burner and also burns more evenly. The round wick burner produces no sooty smoke and virtually no smell.
The Karlskrona Lampfabrik has been operating from the South Swedish harbour town of the same name since 1884 and thanks to its extensive experience produces paraffin lamps with centre draught burners of the highest quality. Paraffin lamps still have decisive advantages over electric light sources: they work without a nearby source of electricity, they can be used in times of crisis, and they create a pleasantly warm, romantic light.
Note:
Replacement glass cylinders can be purchased from our special order department.
More light, no soot. Karlskrona kerosene lamps
In the evolution of non-electric light sources, kerosene lamps are in an advanced position - especially those with a round wick or cosmos burner. It is equipped with a flat, wide wick, which is fed from the tank into the burner in such a way that it emerges from it in a circle at the top. The light yield is thus incomparably higher than with a flat burner, and at the same time the combustion is cleaner: the round wick burner does not soot and hardly smells.
The Karlskrona Lampfabrik, which has been based and active in the southern Swedish port city of the same name since 1884 and thus has a fair amount of experience, manufactures such petroleum lamps with cosmos burners of the highest quality. That they can hold their own to this day next to electric light sources has good reasons, among which are first and foremost a tangible shortage (no electricity nearby), the independence of electricity in times of crisis (self-sufficiency) and the pleasantly warm light (romance).

product_176.description:
General Information
High-powered lamp. Petromax. The eponymous model. Since 1910.
Petromax was developed at the beginning of the last century by Berlin’s councilor of commerce, Max Graetz, named “Petroleum Maxe,” of Ehrich & Graetz.?With all of its accessories it is much more than simply a continually operating emergency light: due to its impressive light output of 400 watts, it can serve as an energy independent, truly high performing light source for gardens and patios (the German military and the Federal Agency for Technical Relief use the lamps as work lights during their deployments), and the separately contained cooktops reliably replace camping stoves with gas cartridges. Operation is truly uncomplicated: you attach the gas mantle, fill the tank with clean petroleum and set, by activating the pump attached to the foot of the lamp, the necessary pressure (this can be read on the manometer that has been attached at the filling opening). A carburetor leads the petroleum into the gas mantle, on whose surface the burning takes place. Ignition ensues by a simple contraption for preheating: on top of the petroleum tank attached is a small bowl, into which you can pour some spiritus; at ignition, the spiritus flam warms the petroleum. (Alternatively, the Petromax is also equipped with a rapid quick-igniter.) We must point out that Petromax produces strong operational noises; you’ll always hear how it works.

With accessories and replacement parts: funnel, filling can, tool set with needle key, nozzle and nozzle needle, manometer gasket and 2 gas mantles (without thorium). product_178.description:
General Information
Discover unique products designed exclusively by Manufactum and made especially for us according to our specifications – you will find these products exclusively at Manufactum.
Just Add Wicks and Floats.
The kind of oil lamp that can be ready for use in a flash: Fill a suitable vessel with water and add a thimbleful of pure vegetable oil. Then push a wick into a cork float (can repeatedly be used) and place it just on the surface of the oil before igniting the wick. With just 10 ml of oil, the floating wick will burn for two hours, with one litre of salad oil, around 200 hours; all this with virtually no soot, no odour, and only as much carbon dioxide as is produced by the growth of plants. When the wick is exhausted, it is simply replaced. We offer short night light wicks made of cotton yarn, encased with paraffin and beeswax, as well as three-leafed cork floats by Glafey of Nuremberg. Both have been produced since 1867 and, as the manufacturer had already trumpeted at the beginning of the 20th century, they are "a must in every reputable establishment." The fact that they still exist after more than 150 years is a guarantee of their quality.
Let there be lightness: a self-made oil lamp.
Light is elementary: The book of Genesis begins with the words "Let there be light", and the taming of fire is regarded as mankind’s earliest cultural achievement. One of the oldest artificial light sources is the oil lamp, which is not only still used today because of its pleasant glow. It is popular, above all, because it can be produced very simply – almost with materials at hand. A suitable vessel for the oil may be found in a variety of forms in the home. Ultimately, any small heat-resistant glass can serve the purpose and, moreover, can be returned to service in the kitchen after being used as a light (and subsequently being washed-up). The fuel is also ever-present in the form of vegetable oil. Vegetable oil is – unlike petroleum-based lamp oil – not only inexpensive and non-toxic but also safe to handle, since it does not burn without the addition of a wick. Thus, even if a lighted oil lamp filled with vegetable oil is tipped over, it does not cause any damage (apart from a grease spot).
Tradition of efficiency. Glafey
Glafey in Nuremberg is a proven expert in the field of candles with wick holders. Thanks to operating experience dating back to 1808, these candles are functionally perfected: they burn with little soot, are odorless and produce exactly the right amount of light for a long burning time. The wick and wick wax are also precisely matched to these requirements.
During production, care has always been taken to use raw materials efficiently and sparingly. For example, the tealights, which have been produced unchanged for decades and whose pack of 12 uses just one tinplate bowl that can be refilled again and again - the refill pack is supplied without a bowl. Or the cork floats and wicks, which have been produced since 1867 (and are only available separately from us), which can be made into fully-fledged oil lights with minimal use of materials and "on-board resources" (glass jar and vegetable oil).
Glafey also relies on plastic-free outer packaging made from cardboard and glassine. In production, Glafey obtains heat from a combined heat and power plant, in which the fuels used are converted particularly efficiently into usable energy, and electricity from 3,000 square meters of solar modules on the company's own roof - which means that one of the oldest light sources is produced under the most modern conditions.
Responsible economic operator for the EU

5 floats (height 6.5 mm, Ø 4 cm) in a glassine paper bag.

product_182.description:
General Information
Classic shape. New technology
LED filament lamp in the form of the classic incandescent lamp known in common parlance as the "light bulb."
LED Filament Bulbs with Glass Support.
What lights these luminants turns out to be a complex construction on closer inspection: You find a so-called substrate (a carrier made of glass) densely covered with a multitude of tiny chip-diode pairs and a fluorescent layer on these diodes consisting mainly of phosphor. In terms of luminous efficacy, light colour and colour rendering, the phosphorous layer provides light properties that come very close to those of the former incandescent light bulbs banned by EU regulation. Besides, LED filament bulbs exceedingly outdo their forerunners in energy efficiency and average service life; therefore, they are a fully-fledged replacement for the traditional incandescent light bulbs.
Close to the Forerunners’ Design. For good reason.
The striking resemblance of the LED filament bulbs shown here to classic types of incandescent bulbs has quite banal technical reasons. Firstly, this is why these bulbs fit into all luminaires with standard sockets (E27, E14). Secondly, in this way, they are able to provide light beams at the same angle as classic incandescent bulbs. And the latter’s light output was the basis for blueprinting the lighting design of most luminaires in use. LED filament bulbs, therefore, can fully replace or may even surpass their discarded “ancestors” in all respects.

General Information
Discover unique products designed exclusively by Manufactum and made especially for us according to our specifications – you will find these products exclusively at Manufactum.
Safety at every turn
Whether it's a heavy, hand-woven wool rug or a lightweight cotton runner - depending on the carpet pad, you can really slip on it. Anti-slip underlays for carpets prevent such slapstick interludes. However, they are usually made of plastic or do not fit under your carpet. We have found a manufacturer that produces anti-slip carpet underlays entirely from renewable raw materials and without plasticizers. A very wide jute fabric is simply coated with natural latex. On stone floors, marble, cork and parquet or even on laminate and PVC, the fabric provides a non-slip surface for any carpet - really any carpet. Because what doesn't fit is made to fit: the anti-slip carpet pad can be easily cut to the size of your carpet. Remember to leave a bit of the carpet overhanging so that the carpet pad remains invisible. The latex carpet pad also increases walking comfort as it is slightly cushioning. It can also be washed, leaves no residue and is also suitable for floors with underfloor heating. It should only not be placed on freshly sealed floors.

product_200.description:
General Information
Carpets made from recycled plastic. Suitable for everyday use - indoors and outdoors
PET plastic bottles, which are still produced in large quantities but are not recycled to the same extent, are hard-wearing, waterproof and durable. This gave Tina and Asad Mirza from the Hamburg-based design label liv interior the idea of producing carpets from recycled PET (rPET). This is because these properties extend their range of use many times over compared to carpets made from natural materials such as cotton or virgin wool. They are unaffected by moisture, so it doesn't matter if a glass tips over during a meal. Even when used on balconies and terraces, rPET carpets can withstand a shower without any consequences. They can be wiped clean or, in the case of heavy soiling, can be washed in the washing machine at up to 40 °C without any problems and are then dry again in a flash. The feel is also impressive: compared to cotton carpets, your feet will hardly notice any difference. The rPET carpets just seem to be woven a little more tightly and feel surprisingly soft. Available as a rug and runner, each in two sizes, as well as a mat.
From the bottle to the thread
The carpets are manufactured in India. The PET bottles collected there are mechanically shredded in recycling plants, the flakes are cleaned of labels and other residues, melted down and stretched into long threads. Like threads made from natural materials, these can also be twisted into yarn and wound onto bobbins. Depending on the size, 100 to 750 recycled PET bottles are required for one carpet. The carpets are hand-woven, so there may be slight variations in size (±5%) and there may be knotted thread ends on the reverse side due to a change of thread. This does not affect the quality of the rug.
Responsible economic operator for the EU

100% polyester, hand-woven and dyed. Yarn count Nm 2/4. Fabric weight 1,700 g/sqm. Machine wash on a gentle cycle up to 40 °C. Do not tumble dry. Made in India. 60 × 90 cm. Weight 980 g.

product_202.description:
General Information
Carpets made from recycled plastic. Suitable for everyday use - indoors and outdoors
PET plastic bottles, which are still produced in large quantities but are not recycled to the same extent, are hard-wearing, waterproof and durable. This gave Tina and Asad Mirza from the Hamburg-based design label liv interior the idea of producing carpets from recycled PET (rPET). This is because these properties extend their range of use many times over compared to carpets made from natural materials such as cotton or virgin wool. They are unaffected by moisture, so it doesn't matter if a glass tips over during a meal. Even when used on balconies and terraces, rPET carpets can withstand a shower without any consequences. They can be wiped clean or, in the case of heavy soiling, can be washed in the washing machine at up to 40 °C without any problems and are then dry again in a flash. The feel is also impressive: compared to cotton carpets, your feet will hardly notice any difference. The rPET carpets just seem to be woven a little more tightly and feel surprisingly soft. Available as a rug and runner, each in two sizes, as well as a mat.
From the bottle to the thread
The carpets are manufactured in India. The PET bottles collected there are mechanically shredded in recycling plants, the flakes are cleaned of labels and other residues, melted down and stretched into long threads. Like threads made from natural materials, these can also be twisted into yarn and wound onto bobbins. Depending on the size, 100 to 750 recycled PET bottles are required for one carpet. The carpets are hand-woven, so there may be slight variations in size (±5%) and there may be knotted thread ends on the reverse side due to a change of thread. This does not affect the quality of the rug.
Responsible economic operator for the EU

product_206.description:
General Information
Inspires the imagination. Robust and down-to-earth
Furniture is beautiful in the children's room - and yet the floor often exerts the greater attraction on your child. The large surface simply offers children more space to play with dolls and cuddly toys, wooden trains and fire engines on a grand scale. An Austrian manufacturer produces this robust cork carpet so that your child can play out all their creative ideas on a hard-wearing surface without sacrificing comfort.
Pure cork - obtained from Portuguese cork oaks - is used for the top side of the rug, while cork granules are laminated onto a cotton backing for the underside. The cork surface is characterized by a particularly warm, cuddly feel, so that your child can stretch out comfortably on the rug from an early age (although we do not guarantee a nap). The underside ensures that the rug is stable and non-slip and is also suitable for underfloor heating. And you will appreciate its sound-absorbing properties at the latest when your child starts jumping and dancing. The easy-care surface can also be wiped clean so that traces of minor mishaps - a spilled superhero drink or an overly enthusiastic coloring book that has been filled in over the edge - can be removed with a damp cloth.
The lovingly designed animal illustrations running all the way around make the children's rug an eye-catcher that also inspires the imagination. The illustrations are applied using UV digital printing and, with their subtle red-brown tones, they have a high lightfastness (5-7) and will accompany your child into their fantasy worlds for a long time. Incidentally, the material thickness of around four millimetres gives the cork rug an impressive additional benefit: It is thick enough to be used as a large pin board - should your growing child one day consider it beneath their dignity to play on the floor. But until then, there will probably be a lot more balls and diggers rolling across the carpet ...

General Information
Patternally Scandinavian: the clear stripe pattern of the hand-woven carpet frames the textile designer Lisbet Friis with bright red woven ends. At the Danish family-owned company Fabula, Scandinavian design meets oriental craftsmanship - the kilim weave means that the weft thread forms the pattern on both sides of the rug, making it usable on both sides. Thanks to its low pile height ROSEMARY is especially suitable for use in passageways and hallways. Made in India.
Carpet care
We recommend using a carpet carpet pad to make the carpet last longer. A carpet carpet pad ensures that the carpet stays in one place. It also reduces the risk of stains. Do not expose your rug to direct sunlight. Since rugs are hand-woven, irregularities in colors and weave may occur. Daily cleaning: vacuum your rug as needed. Do not vacuum your rug with the brushes of your vacuum cleaner brush extended. You can also shake out your carpet. Please do not tap the carpet. Cleaning stains, wool carpets only: Gently dab the spot with a cloth dipped in carbonated water. Thorough cleaning: We recommend professional cleaning.

product_212.description:
General Information
Soft virgin wool. Robust structure
The special weave turns the soft virgin wool into a firm, voluminous carpet one centimeter thick. Strong cotton yarn is used as the warp, and in the weft the thick wool yarn forms "bobbles" or nubs in places, creating a distinctive texture that feels pleasantly cushiony underfoot. Combined with the mottled gray tones, this creates a beautiful, vibrant surface. Nevertheless, the carpet fits well into any style of living - whether minimalist and Scandinavian clear or colorful playful.
The wool carpet is woven in India, where Finarte has been working with hand weavers since the 1990s and thus supports not only the local people, but also the continuation of the traditional weaving craft. The new wool comes from Egypt, where it is obtained mulesing-free. Pure new wool is extremely suitable for carpets: the hard-wearing natural material is abrasion-resistant, lint-free and, thanks to the scaly surface of the wool fibers, also dirt-repellent and has a self-cleaning effect. Regular vacuuming or careful beating is therefore sufficient; in the case of larger soiling, it is recommended to take the carpet to the cleaners.
Finarte. Inventor of a classic
Who hasn't heard of the colorful Finnish rag rug - but its inventor Eija Rasinmäki is less well known. Ever since she was given a loom by her mother, herself a weaver, at a young age, she has been enthusiastic about carpet weaving and later turned her passion into a profession. From the very beginning, back in 1970, she used recycled cotton or wove from remnants - long before the term upcycling was coined. Together with her husband, she founded Finarte in 1985 to offer affordable yet high-quality rugs produced in a resource-conserving way. While she initially designed all of her rugs herself, she now works with a range of different designers. The common thread in her designs is the combination of traditional Finnish weaving craftsmanship with modern Finnish design.
Saving water through upcycling
Since the 1990s, Finarte has had its carpets manufactured in India, a conscious decision for the production location: where the cotton is grown, processed and upcycled, it should also be woven. The company obtains selvedge remnants, production overhangs and offcuts from the textile industry, recycles them and then weaves them into carpets. This saves around 11,000 liters of water per kilogram of recycled cotton - the amount that would be needed to produce one kilogram of fresh cotton. In upcycling, a wide variety of cotton scraps, mostly from the clothing industry, are shredded into fibers and spun into new yarn. In addition to recycled and upcycled cotton, Finarte uses other natural materials such as virgin wool, jute and leather scraps, and since 2018 has also been producing carpets from PET material obtained from recycled plastic bottles.

Rangi za Africa. The colors of Africa
The name says it all: Finarte calls this kilim carpet Mombasa. With its warm rust-redbrauntones, it is reminiscent of the red earth of Africa, while the muted blues, greens and ochres evoke the vastness of the savannah and the beach on the Indian Ocean. This color scheme is no accident, as the design was created in collaboration with the Finnish fair trade label Mifuko. The influence of Kenyan tradition and craftsmanship is based on the close ties of the two Mifuko founders to the country and its people and is evident in all designs. However, like all Finarte carpets, the carpet is woven in India. Thanks to the traditional kilim technique there, in which the pattern is created on both sides of the carpet, it can be used on both sides. A small but fine detail is formed by the knotted fringes. The carpet can be used anywhere in the home, and since it is flat woven (pile height 0.5 cm), it is also suitable for passageways and hallways. The carpet is woven by hand, so small irregularities in color, weave and size may occur. Should stains ever stray onto the carpet, we recommend treating them with (a little) carbonated water and gently dabbing with a cloth. For more thorough cleaning, please take the carpet to professional cleaning.

product_215.description:
General Information
Beach and vacation feeling included. Hand woven bast mat
This Indian bast mat is made on old hand looms. For this, two natural materials are combined: Strong yarn made of organic cotton is used in the warp, and the strong fibers of banana leaves are used in the weft. The result is a robust, yet pleasantly soft mat that can be used in a variety of ways: in the bedroom and bathroom, in the kitchen, hallway and hallway, or on the balcony and terrace. Due to its light weight and because the mat can be easily rolled up, it is also ideal for traveling - in the camper, on the beach or for sunbathing on the lawn.
If you use the raffia mat on tiles, we recommend an anti-slip pad. The mat is quite durable thanks to the easy-care materials and muted colors. If necessary, it can be wiped with a damp cloth or even washed once at 30 ° C.
Care By Me. Danish design, traditional craftsmanship
Behind the Danish label Care By Me are designer Camilla Gullits and her business partner Pernille Pold. Their designs combine Danish design and the traditional craftsmanship of India and Nepal, as their aim is not only to offer high-quality and durable clothing and home textiles, but also to produce them in a resource-friendly and fair way. In Nepal, for example, handmade textiles make up a large part of the national economy and, as in India, the production of textiles is traditionally in the hands of women. Care By Me therefore works with small workshops where women can learn and practise the traditional craft in order to provide them with a secure income. The new wool comes from the region around Kathmandu and is also spun there. The cotton used comes from controlled organic cultivation and Care By Me sources it from a GOTS and fair trade-certified partner company.
Note:
Certain manufacturing steps are carried out by hand. Slight dimensional and color deviations may therefore occur.

product_224.description:
General Information
Often decorative strips in their composition fit only a limited period, preferably a high festival such as Easter, Christmas or Sukkot, or a particular season. Therefore, we have developed a handmade decorative strip and separate motifs, which frees you from such dependencies: Our decoration strip made of solid oak as well as our matching wooden motifs offer you the possibility to design in harmony with the occasion, season and interior over and over again.
Maximum minimalism. For creative freedom in time and space
Over the entire length of 50 cm, four narrow grooves run through a strip of untreated, smoothly sanded oak wood, which already has a high decorative value with its velvety surface and striking grain. The solid natural material promises durable functionality, in which the grooves running in rows allow for a design with depth effect. Above all, the design in the straightforward Scandinavian style corresponds to a maximum minimalism, which opens up the greatest freedom for you with its versatility. Because the neatly milled grooves can be equipped again and again with elements of your choice: with cheeky postcards, romantic letters, combined with leaves and flowers, folded origami or felted decoObjekten - or even with our matching motifs cut from poplar plywood, which form a variably arrangeable, spatially effective backdrop.
Innovative. Manufactum product design
Creating "living products" - i.e. products that integrate into your life, enrich your everyday life and are allowed to age with dignity - is a goal that is close to the heart of our product designer Markus Stallberg. The focus of his designs is therefore on the innovative added value that a product offers you - and the innovation consists of solving a problem that arises in our everyday lives.
"You don't stumble across good ideas," emphasizes Markus Stallberg. Rather, he approaches the solution to such an everyday problem in many small steps, the direction of which is determined by constant observation and questioning. Until a functional solution has been developed, you have to "sometimes go astray". Trial and error, reconsideration and further improvements are just as much a part of this process as a lively exchange with a wide variety of people. An open ear for their respective needs is essential in order to create a product that is functional and yet not too complex. Close cooperation with experienced manufacturers is just as important. After all, the product should not only have an appealing, integrable design on paper, on the computer and in the self-built model, but should also be well crafted and manufactured with care. Instead of reinventing the wheel, the tried and tested can be transferred into the present - with an additional benefit that ideally "satisfies everyone". Life will decide whether this succeeds in the best possible way. And therefore you.

product_228.description:
General Information
Imaginative fun
If your children cast a covetous eye on this decorative strip, don't be surprised. After all, the strip was originally developed as a toy: to support our offspring in their free play in accordance with the principles of Montessori education, to allow them to develop their individual potential and to train their motor and cognitive skills. We are now convinced that the strip also has great decorative qualities and that you can give free rein to your own imagination by placing - and repositioning - the treetops as you wish.
Each of the five treetops has a different shape - hemisphere, cone, ellipse, column or umbrella - so that you can achieve a different effect with each new combination. In addition to the visual experience, the decorative strip offers you an equally fine tactile pleasure when you rearrange it: The base is made of fine-pored maple wood, the tree trunks and crowns are made of beech wood and all surfaces have been sanded and oiled by hand to a velvety smooth finish. And if you're not adding other decorative ideas to your delicate yet solid tree arrangement - such as twigs, leaves and flowers, colorful cards, origami or felt objects - you can of course let the younger members of your family try out a new combination.
The story of the forest. Told by a toy
The Polish family business Wooden Story stands for toys made from certified wood. As befits a family from the forests of the Makov Beskids, Wooden Story also begins with a forest spirit - at least its name. Slavic mythology tells of the forest spirit Borowy, who protects forests and game. Coincidence or not, the founding family of Wooden Story is also called Borowy, and under the expert hands of grandfather Borowy, the company's first wooden toy was created in 1969.
Now in its fourth generation, the family business, which has since established itself with its natural wood furniture, is once again manufacturing wooden toys. The joy of creating for children and the respectful attitude towards nature are reflected in these toys. Wooden Story produces exclusively from certified wood of European origin, to which natural pigments lend color. And instead of sealing artificial varnishes, the surface is given a velvety polish with beeswax and vegetable oils, which emphasizes the natural grain of the wood and preserves its special feel.
Every wooden toy from Wooden Story tells a little story of the forest, naturally and safely. For the protection and enjoyment of the child (and many an adult), as the forest spirit Borowy could not have wished for better.

product_246.description:
General Information
Discover unique products designed exclusively by Manufactum and made especially for us according to our specifications – you will find these products exclusively at Manufactum.
Back to the clear form. The Manufactum cuckoo clock
At the end of the 17th century, clock production in the Black Forest developed from the winter sideline of a few farmers and eventually became the precision engineering center of Germany. The (unjustly) often mocked cuckoo clock was also refined into a quality clock there. The basic shape of its case, which is still common today, goes back to a design competition held in 1850 by Robert Gerwig - head of the Grand Ducal Baden Clockmaking School in Furtwangen and master builder of the Gotthard and Black Forest railroads. The winner was the Karlsruhe architect and professor of design theory Friedrich Eisenlohr. He had given the housing the shape of the railroad keeper's cottages he had designed along the Black Forest Railway - which makes sense as it was precisely this Black Forest Railway that opened up the often remote valleys and contributed significantly to the development of precision mechanics in the Black Forest by providing access to the raw material metal. Over the course of time, however, many cuckoo clocks have had to endure all sorts of design nonsense borrowed from the local flora and fauna, in contrast to their originally rather austere form.
Our cuckoo clock: quality from Baden
We have turned back the cuckoo clock. Our version - a custom-made clock from the Black Forest clock manufacturer Rombach & Haas, founded in 1894 - goes even further than the original design in terms of formal clarity. The black lacquered iron weights in the shape of cones are the only classic decorative element. The mechanical movement comes from a precision engineering company in Triberg, which has been manufacturing clock parts and movements since 1856. It is an 8-day movement, which is more complex and expensive to manufacture than a 1-day movement, which is why it is only used in a few cuckoo clocks.
Whistles and bellows. The cuckoo call
In addition to a gong, the striking mechanism activates bellows on two pipes with a time delay, which produces the characteristic "cuckoo call" that has sounded on most cuckoo clocks in the interval of the major third since the 19th century and identifies the clock as a musical automaton. The bowing of the hand-carved bird during the call is also controlled by one of the bellows with its up and down movement.

A Twofold Advantage: Mounted to the Wall, Still Ready at Hand. Plus, Made of Optical Glass.
This mirror comes with a sturdy concertina arm and a frame made from solid, durably chrome-plated brass. The mirror glass consists of a material rarely used for this purpose: optical glass. The manufacturing process of optical glass is rather tricky, and producing the convex shape requires a multi-step routine. Usually, you find optical glass in the form of lenses in loupes and cameras. Lensmakers have to pay a good deal more attention to the purity of the glass when the magnification rates are higher; therefore, they have to reduce air inclusions and impurities to an absolute minimum.
A concertina arm holds this mirror in place just so that you can adjust the reflection to your needs or you can take the mirror in your hand eventually and put it back into its holder afterwards. One side of this mirror simply reflects the image of whatever is in front of it; the other side magnifies the image five times. The manufacturer Windisch, a family business in Barcelona, has specialized in the handcrafted production of mirrors and bathroom utensils made of brass since its foundation in 1934.

product_258.description:
General Information
Odds & Ends
Colorful home textiles made from industrial waste!

When factories dye yarn to weave textiles, they often produce more yarn than is needed - just in case. This means that considerable quantities of yarn are regularly left over, which are normally disposed of. For the textiles in the Odds & Ends collection, Foekje Fleur collects these yarn remnants - exclusively cotton yarns - and uses them to produce home textiles. Dishcloths, dishcloths, washcloths and shower towels in predetermined complex, graphic patterns of overlapping and intersecting lines in different colors and thicknesses. The colors are created depending on the yarns available. And in batches: after sifting through the available yarns, the Dutch designer puts together the eye-catching and finely balanced color combinations for the next batch of the collection. If the yarns run out, individual colors are replaced or a completely new combination is created. Small variations in the color scheme within a batch are therefore planned for, as are slight differences in size due to production. Odds & Ends scarves are made in Portugal and are easily recognizable by their striped hems woven on a jacquard machine. Practically all the scarves are provided with a hanger and are quick-drying. The exceptionally beautifully designed hangers and banderoles with which the scarves are supplied are the work of Dutch illustrator Rachel Sender and make the scarves the ideal gift.

product_259.description:
General Information
Three colors, three combinations
These towels are the result of our collaboration with the Austrian textile company Framsohn. To bring more color and variety into the bathroom, we had something two-tone in mind - like the double-faced blankets in our range, which have different colored sides. It didn't take much convincing to get Framsohn on board for this project. Our Product Manager was soon able to tap into the weaving mill's rich color palette. The final color selection and combination is also a result of the in-house survey, as everyone involved or interested in textiles, colors and design was able to choose their favorite.
The towels are even more interesting because not just two, but three colors are combined. So the choice is yours. Mix and match all the variants or stick to one combination. Of course, all terry towels are the same in terms of quality and workmanship. Framsohn uses cotton from controlled organic cultivation (kbA) and weaves it with three thread systems, as is usual with real terry towelling. The resulting loops on the surface ensure a generous volume (material weight 540 g/sqm) and a large surface area. This means that the towels can absorb a lot of moisture and feel pleasantly soft on the skin. Each one is woven in the respective width and cross-stitched at the seams, which gives it additional dimensional stability.
Incidentally, Framsohn was so enthusiastic about our idea for these two-tone terry towels that they immediately added them to their own range.
Framsohn. Terry goods and home textiles from the Waldviertel region
Framsohn, the name stands for Franz Amstetter & Söhne, in the Waldviertel region of Lower Austria, is a fourth-generation manufacturer of high-quality home textiles and terry towelling. The family business has always attached great importance to its connection with nature and the local people. This attitude is reflected in several factors. For example, Framsohn weaves the terry towelling from organic-certified cotton. All production still takes place at the company's original headquarters. This reduces transportation routes, allows continuous quality control from the thread to the finished product and enables Framsohn to influence all parameters directly and immediately. To document this, Framsohn has been certified in accordance with the Global Organic Textile Standard (GOTS). This sets high standards for the production of textiles made from organically produced natural fibers - across the entire production chain: from the extraction of textile fibers, through their processing and distribution, to ethical and social criteria. Compliance with the standard is reviewed annually and the GOTS certification is re-awarded.

product_260.description:
General Information
Exotic, colorful and non-slip. Terry towels from Japan
Bathroom textiles from Imabari in Japan - recognizable by the typical sewn-in label - enjoy a worldwide reputation. The bathroom textiles from the local manufacturer Murakami Pile are also characterized by a number of special textile techniques. In addition to special weaving techniques, materials such as washi yarn or coal as a mineral dye are used that are unusual in Europe.
The special feature of these cotton terry towels is apparent at first glance: The long loops of the terry cloth fabric come in four different colors. Genuine terry towelling is somewhat more complex to produce anyway, because it is woven with three thread systems (warp, weft and loop). The multi-colored loops therefore require an additional four differently dyed yarns. The terry towels also impress with their non-slip, highly absorbent fabric, which not only dries excellently, but also dries again quickly. So it's not surprising that the test sample in our product manager's family bathroom quickly became her favorite towel and, once washed, has to go straight back to the sink ...
Hospitable by Tradition. Towels from Imabari
60% of towels in Japan are made in the Japanese town of Imabari, in Ehime Prefecture, in the north of Shikoku Island. There are 4,000 looms per less than 160,000 inhabitants here, including over 120 companies that are allowed to produce towels under the "Imabari Towel" quality label. The water used for bleaching the textiles comes from underground flowing springs that are particularly low in lime and heavy metals, especially from the Sōja River - a circumstance that has indirectly promoted the concentration of companies producing bathroom textiles. The use of the soft water makes the towels particularly pliable and at the same time allows dyes to penetrate deep into the textile fibers. The result: exceptionally soft and intensely colored linens. It has always been a tradition in the region around Imabari to support pilgrims who are on the 1,200 km long Shikoku pilgrimage route (one of the most important Buddhist pilgrimage routes) with food, money, but also just towels on their journey - and this hospitality should also be reflected in the texture of the textiles produced here.
One of the mandatory quality criteria for "Imabari Towels" concerns the ability to absorb water: a 1 × 1 cm piece of the fabric must be able to sink to the bottom in the water within five seconds - an indication that the towel is able to absorb water and also other liquids without prior washing. Accordingly, Imabari Towels are characterized by absorbing moisture extremely quickly.

product_263.description:
General Information
Exotic from Japan. Bathroom textiles with washi
The Japanese company Murakami Pile from the Japanese toweling stronghold of Imabari proves that towels made with a proportion of paper yarn - the robust but light and absorbent washi - dry very well. In addition to cotton, the loops of the terry towels are also made of washi. This traditional Japanese paper is made from bast fibers, which are obtained in the best quality (as here) from the Maulberry plant kozo, which is native to Asia, and the two daphne plants mitsumata and gampi. Due to its material structure, washi is softer, lighter and more absorbent, but at the same time more tear-resistant and flexible than traditional Western papers. Its use for textiles is not new: it was already used in earlier times as a lining material - for kimonos, for example.
Murakami buys washi paper from the province of Mino, which consists largely of Philippine kozo, the strongest and thickest of the three fibers. This paper is cut into 2-4 mm wide strips, twisted into yarn and then used for weaving. The positive properties of washi paper are combined with those of the cotton used. In addition, the paper yarns create a light massage effect. Similar to linen, washi also becomes a little softer with every use and every wash. You can also find a matching bath mat in our range.

product_270.description:
General Information
Incredibly soft and fine. Terry towels made from Supima® cotton
Supima® is synonymous worldwide with the highest, finest quality of Pima cotton - it is one of the best extra-long staple cottons available. Only one percent of the cotton harvested worldwide reaches Supima® quality, of which only a few tons come from controlled organic cultivation. This cotton is normally used for fine outerwear or luxurious bed linen, but never for bath and terry products. These terry towels from the Swiss weaving mill Weseta are therefore truly exceptional and rare: they are woven from the same fine Supima® cotton from controlled organic cultivation. Organic cotton usually has a rather "stubbly" dry appearance, as it generally has short fibers. Supima® organically grown cotton, on the other hand, is supple and soft because it has very long fibers - in technical terms, this is called extra-long staple. Terry towels made from it are therefore extremely fine and soft, yet durable.
Light, absorbent, economical
The GOTS-certified terry towels are rather light with an average basis weight of 400 g/sqm, yet very absorbent due to the extraordinary cotton quality with the extra-long fibers and their particularly high fibrillation - this is what the experts call the water drainage capacity. Not only do they dry faster than heavy terry towelling, but more towels can be put in the washing drum or tumble dryer. They also use less water during washing due to their lower volume and grammage. Weseta was able to secure a larger supply of the valuable, rare yarn, which means that the production of these terry towels is not possible indefinitely. The yarn is dyed in Switzerland; weaving and finishing take place at Weseta's company site in Sernftal in the Glarus region - and have been since 1864.

product_272.description:
General Information
Washing with washi. Bathroom textiles with paper
Who would have thought that drying yourself with paper would be particularly good? Or at least with textiles made with a proportion of paper yarns? The company Murakami Pile from the Japanese towel stronghold of Imabari is here to prove it. In addition to cotton, the loops of the terry products consist of a proportion of washi paper - the traditional, robust Japanese paper, which is obtained in the best quality (as here too) from the bast fibers of the Maulberry plant kozo, which is native to Asia, and the two daphne plants mitsumata and gampi. Due to its material structure, washi is softer, lighter and more absorbent, but at the same time more tear-resistant and flexible than traditional Western papers. Its use for textiles is not new: it was already used in earlier times as a lining material - for kimonos, for example.
Murakami buys washi paper from the province of Mino, which consists largely of Philippine kozo, the strongest and thickest of the three fibers. This paper is cut into 2-4 mm wide strips, twisted into yarn and then used for weaving. The positive properties of washi paper are combined with those of the cotton used. In addition, the paper yarns create a light massage effect. Similar to linen, washi also becomes a little softer with every use and every wash. The washi yarn and cotton differ in color, resulting in a mottled shade. We also offer a matching bath mat.
Hospitable by Tradition. Towels from Imabari
60% of towels in Japan are made in the Japanese town of Imabari, in Ehime Prefecture, in the north of Shikoku Island. There are 4,000 looms per less than 160,000 inhabitants here, including over 120 companies that are allowed to produce towels under the "Imabari Towel" quality label. The water used for bleaching the textiles comes from underground flowing springs that are particularly low in lime and heavy metals, especially from the Sōja River - a circumstance that has indirectly promoted the concentration of companies producing bathroom textiles. The use of the soft water makes the towels particularly pliable and at the same time allows dyes to penetrate deep into the textile fibers. The result: exceptionally soft and intensely colored linens. It has always been a tradition in the region around Imabari to support pilgrims who are on the 1,200 km long Shikoku pilgrimage route (one of the most important Buddhist pilgrimage routes) with food, money, but also just towels on their journey - and this hospitality should also be reflected in the texture of the textiles produced here.
One of the mandatory quality criteria for "Imabari Towels" concerns the ability to absorb water: a 1 × 1 cm piece of the fabric must be able to sink to the bottom in the water within five seconds - an indication that the towel is able to absorb water and also other liquids without prior washing. Accordingly, Imabari Towels are characterized by absorbing moisture extremely quickly.

product_274.description:
General Information
Taken from the Hamam
The Turkish steam bath, the hamam, has a rich tradition in the Arab-Mediterranean region and is still an integral part of bathing culture today. For centuries, a visit to a hamam has followed the same ritual sequence, during which visitors pass through various rooms. The temperatures there slowly rise from 30 °C to as high as 55 °C, allowing the circulatory system to adjust to the heat. At the same time, each room serves its own purpose: resting at the beginning, exfoliation and cleansing, relaxing massage, stimulating water showers or nourishing oil baths, and the final resting phase that brings the cleansing ritual to a close. During the hamam visit, visitors are wrapped in a so-called fouta or peshtemal (also pestemal), which are traditionally woven by hand at home or in small businesses. Over the centuries, this has developed into a craft that is passed on and cultivated from generation to generation. Typical features of hamam cloths are the traditional striped patterns and fringes. They are made as a flat cotton fabric, so that they are absorbent on the one hand, but can also dry quickly again. Thanks to these properties, the hamam cloths are not only used in the steam bath, but are also popular as a towel, blanket or scarf.
In this country, the lightweight hamam cloths have also long conquered sauna and bath, beach and garden. Space-saving, absorbent and fast drying, they are also ideal companions for travel or day trips. Our Hamam bath towel comes from the Framsohn weaving mill. It is woven from soft, fine cotton with optional rosé or gray stripes on the natural white, twill-bonded base and shows the typical, here slightly shorter fringes.

product_276.description:
General Information
The silk washing glove is recommended for sensitive skin types. This hammam mitt has a smooth, even texture, without being soft, for an eminently gentle scrub.
Effective Skin Scrub with Water and Kese.
Scrubbing dampened skin is the field of application of the traditional hammam mitt, the kese; and you need no soap or shower gel for the scrubbing. To remove dead skin cells, rub the damp skin with the mitt several times in one direction and then change directions – working either on individual areas of skin or the entire body. Then shower off the loosened skin cells and lather the skin with the soap of your choice. It is not advisable to exfoliate with a kese mitt every day. We recommend using the mitt once a week as part of a basic cleansing routine. Men’s skin is particularly benefitting from this kind of bathing practice.
Kese Made of Purely Natural Materials.
A Turkish family-run business makes our hammam mitts in Bursa, some 100 km south of Istanbul. The staff there make the kese according to traditional methods and apply only first-class materials. The weaving mill uses yarns from pure, natural raw materials – not always the case with this kind of product – and sets store by having the origins precisely traced. Their skilled weaving results in an outstandingly regular weaving pattern; the fabrics have an excellent texture but are none the less robust and long-lasting. You can use them with or without soap.
The Traditional Hammam. Peeling the Skin and Stimulating Its Metabolism.
The traditional Turkish bath, the hammam, dates back hundreds of years. Impressive examples of this ritualistic bathing culture abound in the Arab region are found, for instance, at the Banu Umayya clan’s summer residence of Qasr Amra, 70 kilometres east of Amman, with its baths and famous frescoes. 
However, bathing culture is not just about striking architecture; it is also a sophisticated cultural practice. In a Turkish steam bath, visitors pass through different rooms where the temperature gradually increases from 30 °C to 55 °C to allow their cardio-circulatory system to adjust to the heat without placing the body under unnecessary strain. And each room has its own function: there is an initial relaxation room, a massage room where visitors get their muscles loosened and various beauty treatments cleanse and purify the skin, and finally a room where cool to pleasantly warm water is poured on the skin to increase the blood circulation. Subsequently the visitors round of the bathing ritual in another relaxation area. 
During the massages, a key element of the hammam, the body is rubbed down with a fine wash mitt known as the “kese”, which is made either of silk or goat’s hair. The rub removes dead skin cells and effectively cleanses the skin’s pores which have been opened by the warm steam. Afterwards, the skin glows radiantly, shows a beautiful, clear complexion and feels soft and smooth.

General Information
In our quest to guarantee you the best possible reliability and functionality in products, at times there is the need to be inventive: our team develops tailor-made solutions in-house or recommends product upgrades corresponding to our guiding principles to associated manufacturers.
Space miracle and order keeper. The Werkhaus classic
This tidy furniture for desk and office is one of the first products from Werkhaus and has already proven itself for more than 20 years with its many compartments of different sizes and arrangements. Especially for us, the manufacturer has also produced them in black.
The organizers provide order and color on the desk. We offer them in two sizes with eight or 16 compartments, in which papers and office or other indispensable utensils can be clearly arranged within easy reach.
Werkhaus. Peg and Wedge Connectors 2.0.
The intelligent Werkhaus construction principle is astonishingly simple and needs no tools for assembly: The robust, shape-retaining HDF (high-density fiberboard) elements consist of panels made from fine wood fiber, glue and water. Precisely cut with CNC machines, the pieces fit together easily. You connect them by inserting a peg notched on both sides of one panel through a slot in a second panel. Then you fasten the peg with a rubber ring. The resulting lightweight units are astonishingly stable – despite relatively thin walls. While highly practical in use, they tolerate dismantling and reassembling at any time.
The reversible connection technology, the choice of materials and the machine manufacturing process allow for the construction of complex, at the same time very inexpensive products predestined for sales displays in stores and trade fairs. Unsurprisingly, this kind of furniture rapidly became the main business of the 1992 founded firm.
Lots of Drawers. Ready with Little Effort.
Thanks to the precise cutting and the clean machine processing, the affordable furnishings can be constructed from only 3 to 6 mm thin boards. Such furniture would be much more difficult and therefore much more expensive to produce by carpenters. Besides, the visible plug-in connections of peg, wedge and rubber rings create a unique design language, particularly evident in the monochrome versions. Werkhaus develops and manufactures all its products at its headquarters in Lower Saxony. We deliver individual parts; however, we are sure you’ll find the assembling an easy undertaking.

General Information
All weathers: cast metal from the Black Country and glass domes from Worcestershire
This outdoor wall lamp with right-angled bent cable-carrying tube combines in itself a functional design with robust materials and craftsmanship. Thanks to its weather resistance, it is just overqualified for private domestic use. The castings come from a small foundry in the Black Country, the ore and coal region of the West Midlands. They are made of galvanized cast iron and are created using the sand casting process, or lost mold. The neatly fitted glass domes come from a glassblowing workshop in Worcestershire, where traditional glassmaking continues, preserving the once-famous English glass tradition.
Davey Lighting. Luminaires made in England
The roots of Davey Lighting go back to London's West Indies ports, where the hardware and ship lighting company (then called Davey & Co) began operations in 1885. Soon its functional lights were in use on many ships. As the glory days of British seafaring faded in the 20th century, Davey used the skills he had acquired over decades to produce what were originally maritime lights for use on land - initially in industrial and commercial settings.
However, the range was soon taken up by architects and designers, which is hardly surprising, since Davey's luminaires are still distinguished today by what characterized them even in their founding days: a clear design language oriented to purpose, a robustness conveyed through the choice of materials, and a workmanship with attention to every detail that was indispensable for the original use in maritime or industrial environments. From the cast iron, to the turned or pressed metal parts, to the hand-blown glass domes, all components are made by specialized craftsmen in England. Even the textile-covered cables that equip some of the lights are made near Davey's current headquarters in the Cotswolds.

product_316.description:
General Information
Winter can come - and stay outside
This extraordinary curtain is made of heavy, dense and at the same time very voluminous loden. Hung in the entrance area in front of the door or window, it is a real protective shield against the cold and draughts. The curtain owes its ability to insulate heat exceptionally well to several factors. Loden is woven from so-called carded yarn, which is voluminous and slightly curly due to the special spinning technique. For our loden, the yarn is spun from pure new wool, which itself already has good heat-insulating properties, with a generous amount of material and woven very densely: this also results in the high basis weight of 1,000 g/ running meter. In addition, the normally smooth loden is heavily roughened so that the volume is significantly increased and even more heat-insulating air can be trapped. Traditionally, such a thick, fluffy fabric is called a frieze.
Our wool frieze is woven in the Gebrüder Mehler cloth factory in Tirschenreuth. Founded in 1644, the textile factory still carries out all stages of processing under one roof, from spinning and weaving to dyeing, finishing and making up. The heat protection curtain is ready-made and fitted with ten large, sturdy eyelets (39.5 mm Ø inside) made of stainless steel (as are otherwise used for truck tarpaulins) so that it can be easily pulled over a pole. With a width of 150 cm, it is ideal for standard doors (H 200 × W 100 cm), for which we recommend a rod length of 120 cm. For wider doors or double doors, you can simply hang two curtains next to each other.

product_326.description:
General Information
Tufted. Bathmats.
The beauty of these mats lies in the tufting. The backing is "injected" with ring spun long staple cotton fibers. They are held with special "grip arms" so that it creates a thick pile on both sides. The subsequent loops are then cut on one side thus creating an open velour on one side and a closed loop on the other. The mat shows on each side the negative of the other side. The pile is washed first at the weaving mill where the backing in the warp and weft come together differently thus making the fabric more tense and less likely to shrink. This works best by this type of heavy fabric with a weight of 2,100 g/ sm and a thickness of almost 20 mm. 100% cotton.

General Information
Colorful bath mat, inspired by the blooming tulip fields of the Netherlands. Soft to the touch and pleasant to the feet, the pure cotton terry fabric is made exclusively from yarn left over from the textile industry and brings color into the bathroom. It matches the towels in the collection, but is a real eye-catcher in combination with monochrome bathroom textiles and a particularly attractive way of avoiding waste.
Odds & Ends
Colorful home textiles made from industrial waste! When factories dye yarn to weave textiles, they often produce more yarn than is needed - just in case. This means that considerable quantities of yarn are regularly left over, which are normally disposed of. For the textiles in the Odds & Ends collection, Foekje Fleur collects these yarn remnants - exclusively cotton yarns - and uses them to produce home textiles. Dishcloths, dishcloths, washcloths and shower towels in predetermined complex, graphic patterns of overlapping and intersecting lines in different colors and thicknesses. Their colors are created depending on the yarns available. And in batches: after sifting through the available yarns, the Dutch designer puts together the eye-catching and finely balanced color combinations for the next batch of the collection. If the yarns run out, individual colors are replaced or a completely new combination is created. Small variations in the color scheme within a batch are therefore planned for, as are slight differences in size due to production. Odds & Ends scarves are made in Portugal and are easily recognizable by their striped hems woven on a jacquard machine. Practically all of the scarves have a hanger and are quick-drying. The exceptionally beautifully designed hangers and banderoles with which the scarves are supplied are the work of Dutch illustrator Rachel Sender and make the scarves the ideal gift.

This Indian bast mat is made on old hand looms. For this, two natural materials are combined: Strong yarn made of organic cotton is used in the warp, and the strong fibers of banana leaves are used in the weft. The result is a robust, yet pleasantly soft mat that can be used in a variety of ways: in the bedroom and bathroom, in the kitchen, hallway and hallway, or on the balcony and terrace. Care By Me. Danish design, traditional craftsmanship
Behind the Danish label Care By Me are designer Camilla Gullits and her business partner Pernille Pold. Their designs combine Danish design and the traditional craftsmanship of India and Nepal, as their aim is not only to offer high-quality and durable clothing and home textiles, but also to produce them in a resource-friendly and fair way. In Nepal, for example, handmade textiles make up a large part of the national economy and, as in India, the production of textiles is traditionally in the hands of women. Care By Me therefore works with small workshops where women can learn and practise the traditional craft in order to provide them with a secure income. The new wool comes from the region around Kathmandu and is also spun there. The cotton used comes from controlled organic cultivation and Care By Me sources it from a GOTS and fair trade-certified partner company.

General Information
Greetings from the Danish Broadcasting Headquarters.
Vilhelm Lauritzen, one of the most important Danish architects and a pioneering representative of Danish functionalism, was a master in combining material and light. Throughout his life, he worked according to the credo: "No life without aesthetics". He designed this lamp in the mid-1940s for the Danish broadcasting headquarters. Even then it was produced by Louis Poulsen and quickly became one of their best-selling models. In an exemplary manner, its design follows Lauritzen's basic idea of combining directed light that casts shadows with diffuse light. Directed light falls downwards through the opening in the base of the shade, while the mouth-blown shade itself radiates an even and soft light into the room. Three layers of glass, an inner layer of clear glass, a middle layer of white glass and an outer layer of clear glass, build the shade of a luminaire suitable for both high and low mounting. Louis Poulsen resumed the production in 2016 after bringing the lighting technology and energy consumption up to date.

product_346.description:
General Information
Natural glass form: Drop-shaped opal glass lamp by Wilhelm Braun-Feldweg.
Wilhem Braun-Feldweg, a leading post-war industrial designer, invented these opal glass lamps in 1959. Braun-Feldweg based his design on the drop-like bubbles that are formed in glass-blowing. product_351.description:
General Information
From England: Bone China Lamps.
‘Bone China’ is one of the noblest porcelains. It’s a bright white, extremely thin yet practically unbreakable. Its most surprising property is perhaps the way it lets through the light – shimmering like satin and with a warm glow. The secret Chinese recipe for making bone china was cracked by a stone factory in England in the middle of the 18th century – the addition of bone ash in the firing process. This, and other ingredients like quartz-sand, render the whole production process far from easy. Mass-production is impossible, and the number of firms that have the necessary manufacturing skills is limited. We’ve found such a firm in England that possesses real ‘craftsman skills!
British, in Detail. Lamps from BTC.
Lamps made by BTC (= British Timeless Classics), in the vicinity of Oxford, have attained the status of timeless classics. The creative spirit and driving force behind the firm is Peter Bowles, who pursues his very clear idea and just as clearly realises his agenda. The process starts with the manufacture: Bowles wants to produce lamps that are British down to the level of detail. For example, the bone china-lamp shades come from a pottery in Stoke-on-Trent, known as the "the Potteries" because of the almost 500 potteries that used to be located there. Almost all are gone today and the firm, which also belongs to Bowles, would not exist except for BTC. He took it over when it was on the brink of bankruptcy and has restructured it while keeping all the employees. The hand-blown glass domes come from a glass blowing shop in Worcestershire which Bowles also bought. In addition to domes for lamps, the shop produces coloured glass windows for historical buildings and churches. A handful of glass blowers with their two small smelting furnaces practice the methods of glass blowing and uphold the once famous English tradition of this trade. The British manufacture of the lamps extends to the cables, too. Bowles was dissatisfied with the plastic wrapped cables on his first lamp, so he used a locally produced cloth wrapped cable from a clothes iron for his exhibition piece. The reaction was so positive that he has used cloth cable since. They are locally produced near the firm in home-based work.

product_352.description:
General Information
Of Light and Shapes.
Porcelain in general and the even more translucent bone china, that complex mixture of kaolin, feldspar, silica sand and more than 50% bone ash developed in the 18th century in England, is used especially for ornament purposes. The ornament can be controlled by varying the thickness of the material or by altering the refraction by folding. These are characteristics Peter Bowles can use. In addition to the immediately visible, substantive design of the bone china objects a second gestalt effect emerges when the source of light in the lampshade is turned on. In contrast to the cream coloured shape in the unlit state, the lampshade becomes a rich yellow with clearly identifiable outlines when the lamp is lit.
Pleated Porcelain.
Whether the so-called pleated lamps follow a whim of Peter Bowles or pick up on the design of the often pleated classical lampshades made of silk is secondary. The effect displays the ribbed lamps, which spaciously surround the bulb with their convex shapes, in a uniquely beautiful way: since the ribs are not parallel but arranged to suggest something agreeably proportioned and round inside, the range of thickness of the walls is considerable and the degree of penetration of light yet more manifold. product_358.description:
General Information
Curved folds
A special feature of these vases are the folds that are "curved" into the glass using traditional craftsmanship. The production of a folded vase is complex and requires the teamwork of well-coordinated glassmakers. After the heated, viscous glass mass has been blown into a spherical, hollow bowl, it is passed on to the glassmaker's pipe for the second work step. In this step, another glassmaker blows the bowl into a conical shape by adding additional glass mass, which is distributed ("set") accordingly, and transfers it from the pipe to a basting iron. In the third step, the glass is thrown open by vigorously rotating the basting iron around its own axis until it takes on the shape of an open flower; the subsequent slow, sensitive swinging back and forth of the basting iron works the folds into the flower. Finally, the basting iron is knocked off and the maker's logo is stamped on the smoothed out tear-off point.
This makes each vessel unique - as can be seen from the fact that not all vases are the same height and have exactly the same drapery. Lush bouquets of flowers fall naturally into a decorative arrangement.
A shimmer of green. Thuringian forest glass
The original type of the famous Thuringian Forest glass is blown and cast at Farbglashütte Lauscha in the south of the Thuringian Forest. The glass originally owes its characteristic green shimmer to the high proportion of iron oxides in the sands of the Thuringian Forest. The raw material for this highly prized glass specialty is melted from this sand, potash and lime. Another typical feature of Thuringian Forest glass is the so-called "Gispen", air bubbles trapped in the glass, which characterize the centuries-old production process in front of the furnace.
Note:
Certain manufacturing steps are carried out by hand. Slight dimensional and color deviations may therefore occur.

product_359.description:
General Information
Vide-poche - Don't search, find
Pocket empty, bowl full - this is how the function of this storage bowl can be briefly summarized (French vider: empty, poche: pocket, usually of clothing), which is also known as Gentleman’ s Tray (presumably because the gentleman of yesteryear had no handbag for his small everyday companions). As the name suggests, the bowl preferably holds the contents of a trouser, coat or jacket pocket - small change, keys, phone - and keeps everything within easy reach in the hallway or entrance area, for example. Of course, this requires a certain amount of discipline, as everything has to find its way into the bowl first. But once you've established the habit of emptying your pockets, it saves you a lot of searching ... The Vide-poche can also be used for all other small items that need a designated place when they are not in use, such as on the desk or dining room table, in the kitchen or in the bathroom.
Traditionally, such pocket emptiers were made of porcelain. Our Vide-poche manufactures Sonnenleder from supple, vegetable pit-tanned cowhide - no matter how energetically you empty your pockets, the leather ensures that the small items can be deposited without the loud clattering of porcelain (a definite advantage late at night if you don't want anyone to be startled out of their sleep). The sturdy leather, available in the typical reddish shade of pit-tanned leather or dyed black in the barrel, is double-layered and sewn with neatly turned-in edges. Color-matching leather-covered rivets hold the Vide-poche in a shell shape. As is typical of the material, the leather also takes on an individual patina over time, which is particularly noticeable on the natural-colored leather.
Leather from the pit. Red tanned
Sonnenleder in Bodman-Ludwigshafen on Lake Constance stands for a consistently functional, pure design. The meticulously working company still uses the traditional method of leather production: vegetable pit tanning. Only hides from southern German cattle are used for this. The tanning agents used contain mainly decoctions of bark, roots and fruit. In twelve pits with slightly increasing concentrations of tanning broth, they convert the protein fibers of the cattle hides into leather fibers over a period of six to twelve weeks.
After tanning, the hides are air-dried and greased in a lubrication barrel according to a well-guarded recipe. Undyed, the finished leather has a characteristic, slightly light brown-reddish hue, which also gave the leather the name "red-tanned" and which varies from batch to batch. Use, sun and rain change the color tone, and over time a natural protection forms, the patina, which gives the leather an unmistakable appearance. The leather dyed in the barrel also acquires a shiny patina with use.

product_367.description:
General Information
Recycling used glass. Vases made from wine bottles
What began two years ago in a Parisian apartment as an idea between friends is now a success story. The two Frenchmen Emeric Cruchant Fleuriau and Gauthier Decarne collect empty wine bottles to make glass flower vases in various sizes. A kind of revitalization measure, as they describe it themselves, with which they want to preserve the carefree atmosphere of wine evenings in convivial company. To this end, the two have now entered into a partnership with restaurateurs in the Hauts-de-France region, Decarne's home, who regularly hand over the used glass collected in their restaurants - more than 1,000 bottles a week - to them. The manual part of this undertaking works as follows: The bottles are first thoroughly cleaned and then the neck of the bottle is "blasted off", as they say in glass workers' jargon, i.e. first scored and then cut off with special scissors. The sharp-edged edges that are created during this process are finally sanded clean and smooth. Depending on the initial shape of the bottle and the color of the glass, the vases can turn out differently.
