Its simple solidity provides a striking contrast to the floral splash of color: cast and polished by hand from concrete, this vase highlights the delicate beauty of your small bouquet or individual flowering branches. The low-set center of gravity gives the vase additional stability, and a cork plate attached underneath protects the surfaces of your furniture. You do not have to worry about water stains on the table, dresser or windowsill anyway: the concrete was hydrophobized and is therefore reliably waterproof.
Natural show value. Concrete objects from Beske
Concrete as a building material has long since made its way from exterior architecture into interior design and even into the visual arts - even if there are still certain reservations about the material: It is said to be massive, clunky, more of a block on the leg than a decorative or even artistic object. Complete misconceptions, as the designs cast in concrete by the young Cologne-based Beske manufactory demonstrate. The Beske brothers prefer to work with wood, steel - and concrete, which they cast by hand in painstaking detail. As a building and construction material, concrete is unique anyway: on the one hand, the machine-produced stone is easy to process, extremely stable and so robust that it can last for generations. But above all, and this is particularly important to the Cologne-based manufacturer, concrete consists of the natural raw materials water, sand and gravel with the addition of cement as a binding agent, which means that transportation distances can be kept short. And last but not least, the versatile material is perfect for the manufactory's purist designs, whose clear geometric shapes fit into any room and create striking accents.

A shimmer of green. Thuringian forest glass
The original type of the famous Thuringian Forest glass is blown and cast at Farbglashütte Lauscha in the south of the Thuringian Forest. The glass originally owes its characteristic green shimmer to the high proportion of iron oxides in the sands of the Thuringian Forest. The raw material for this highly prized glass specialty is melted from this sand, potash and lime. Another typical feature of Thuringian Forest glass is the so-called "Gispen", air bubbles trapped in the glass, which characterize the centuries-old production process in front of the furnace.

General Information
The vessels and tableware from the REDE series are inspired by fine porcelain from Japanese culture on the one hand and the structure of fishing nets on the other. The relief on the outside gives the impression of a net encircling the shapes. The shape of the spherical vase is reminiscent of Japanese lanterns and is suitable for voluminous bouquets as well as individual flower stems and branches. The filigree vessel is produced in Galicia and the fine relief is made by hand.
Sargadelos
Tradition and craftsmanship, a fine sense of form and coloration. Sargadelos is a ceramics company with a long history: for over 200 years, the now 200-strong company has been producing high-quality and exquisitely crafted products - including vases, bowls and tableware with finely worked graphic patterns and reliefs - in its two production facilities in Galicia, Spain. To this day, the decorations, which predominantly originate from Celtic and Galician culture, are made by hand, initially using handcrafted templates and then by hand to apply the fine details. And you can see it: the intense colors show fine gradients created by the brush application. The deep cobalt blue that characterizes many of his prints was an early trademark of the company and, in combination with the soft white tone of the ceramics, a true classic. Sargadelos became a valued reference in the world of ceramics in its early history and also attracted attention with collaborations such as the one with David Chipperfield for the REDE tableware series. Today, the Sargadelos Foundation manages the business and attaches great importance to preserving the company's cultural and artistic heritage.
David Chipperfield x Sargadelos
David Chipperfield is an English architect. He founded his architectural practice in London in 1985 under the name David Chipperfield Architects. Buildings such as the Museum of Modern Literature in Marbach, the Neues Museum in Berlin, the Saint Louis Art Museum and the Museo Jumex in Mexico City made the group famous worldwide. His designs are serious and solid, exude dignity and a certain gravitas and integrate the history and memories that belong to the buildings and their surroundings. It is no coincidence that David Chipperfield designed a product series for Sargadelos: the Briton first came to Galicia, the region and headquarters of the Spanish ceramics manufacturer, for a vacation in the 1990s. He loved it, and many more visits followed. Chipperfield appreciates the direct and unadorned nature of the region and its inhabitants, shaped by the rugged nature and the sea. An antithesis to his life in London.

General Information
Beauty with an elegant swing of the hips
Bergs Potter calls this collection "Belle", and the "Beauty" represents its name with the natural grace of organic shapes - matching the handmade production on the potter's wheel, which makes each vase unique. Turning on the potter's wheel leaves fine marks on the ceramic surface that elegantly surround the vase, as characteristic as the annual rings of a tree. Made from majolica clay, the inside of the vase is given a transparent glaze after biscuit firing - the first firing at a moderate temperature - instead of the classic opaque tin glaze, before the body is fired a second time. Natural-colored and unglazed on the outside, the vase has a water-impermeable interior thanks to the inner glaze - ready for lush, colorful bouquets of delicate meadow flowers, magnificent roses, elegant callas or even striking corkscrew willow, forsythia and cherry blossom branches. Whatever pleases your eye, this vase will present it with its own elegant swing of the hips.
Plant pots for generations. Bergs Potter in Copenhagen
When Victor Berg inherited his ceramics business in Copenhagen in 1942, it was particularly important to him to make the everyday lives of his fellow human beings a little more colorful in gray times. In the words of the Danish poet Hans Christian Andersen: "Life alone is not enough, said the butterfly. You must have sunshine, freedom and a little flower." So Berg always kept a bouquet of vases and pots in his store and also added cut flowers to the range. The people of Copenhagen liked this - over the years, several stores in the Danish capital were added, and eventually also plant pots and planters based on his own designs. When Victor Berg's children joined the family business in the 1980s, they began to have their own ideas - initially inspired by historical models that they found all over Europe - molded in terracotta. To this end, Bergs Potter still works with traditional potteries in Tuscany, more precisely in Lucca, and now also in Portugal; a tradition that is now being continued with great dedication by the third generation of Bergs. The preferred material is the famous southern Tuscan Galestro clay, which is rich in minerals and is considered to be particularly frost-resistant. Once fired, even the unglazed terracotta can show shades of red and pink, gray and white - an appealing natural patina that only this clay possesses. Another advantage for the health of your potted plants: the carbonate and potassium salts contained in the clay ensure good permeability, which can have a particularly positive effect on the development of the root system.

Porcelain wants sea
The sea and its tides, wind, weather and waves: The design of the native of East Frisia Anna Badur is created in intense engagement with nature. product_379.description:
General Information
Beauty in organic elegance
Bergs Potter calls this collection "Belle", and the "Beauty" represents its name with the natural grace of organic shapes - in keeping with the hand production on the potter's wheel, which makes each bowl unique. Turning on the potter's wheel leaves fine marks on the ceramic surface that elegantly surround the bowl, as characteristic as the annual rings of a tree. Made from majolica clay, the inside of the bowl is coated with a transparent, food-safe glaze after biscuit firing - the first firing at a moderate temperature - instead of the classic opaque tin glaze, before the body is fired a second time. Natural-colored and unglazed on the outside, the bowls have a water-impermeable inside thanks to the inner glaze. In addition to utensils or felt flowers, you can also use them to store your daily apple or arrange fresh cut flowers.
Plant pots for generations. Bergs Potter in Copenhagen
When Victor Berg inherited his ceramics business in Copenhagen in 1942, it was particularly important to him to make the everyday lives of his fellow human beings a little more colorful in gray times. In the words of the Danish poet Hans Christian Andersen: "Life alone is not enough, said the butterfly. You must have sunshine, freedom and a little flower." So Berg always kept a bouquet of vases and pots in his store and also added cut flowers to the range. The people of Copenhagen liked this - over the years, several stores in the Danish capital were added, and eventually also plant pots and planters based on his own designs. When Victor Berg's children joined the family business in the 1980s, they began to have their own ideas - initially inspired by historical models that they found all over Europe - molded in terracotta. To this end, Bergs Potter still works with traditional potteries in Tuscany, more precisely in Lucca, and now also in Portugal; a tradition that is now being continued with great dedication by the third generation of Bergs. The preferred material is the famous southern Tuscan Galestro clay, which is rich in minerals and is considered to be particularly frost-resistant. Once fired, even the unglazed terracotta can show shades of red and pink, gray and white - an appealing natural patina that only this clay possesses. Another advantage for the health of your potted plants: the carbonate and potassium salts contained in the clay ensure good permeability, which can have a particularly positive effect on the development of the root system.

product_381.description:
General Information
Discover unique products designed exclusively by Manufactum and made especially for us according to our specifications – you will find these products exclusively at Manufactum.
What is possible. Mouth-blown glass.
This bowl is actually still created the way hollow glass was formed in ancient times - in many small steps and with a lot of patience at the glassmaker's pipe, with the help of which the glassmaker repeatedly picks up a new batch of liquid crystal glass from the melting furnace, in order to be able to work the bowl from the so-called Kölbl. He has to keep the pipe constantly moving, turning it and blowing it in again and again until a hollow body is formed. Other tools used by the glassmaker are the wulger wood and the gutter made of wet beech or pear wood, which he uses to shape the hot glass mass. Periodically, he must hold the glass on the pipe in the fire so that he can continue to shape it - if it cools down too much, it becomes tough.
The glassmaker places the hot glass mass, which has been twisted into an elongated shape, in an optical preform made of steel and blows it out until the mass takes on the specified shape and relief-like nubs form. While still hot, the glassmaker then rolls the mass in colored flour, heats it again, and continues shaping with the Wulger wood - the colored glass bonds with the base body. Again, the pipe must always remain in motion, the glassmaker once again picks up crystal glass and, while constantly turning, blows the batch into the finished mold made of beech wood. At the flattened bottom of the bowl, a tack iron is finally pressed on to be able to hold the workpiece further, while on the other side of the glassmaker knocks off the pipe and with the help of the Aufreibschere the strongly heated, still closed edge of the bowl expands and shapes - and turns and turns.
Preserve craft. The glass school in Zwiesel.
At the Zwiesel glass school, this craft is still taught. The school has been in existence since 1904 and its reputation radiates far beyond the borders of the region. At the time of its foundation, it was still located in the middle of the center of the glass industry in Europe, which stretched from the Bavarian Forest to Bohemia. Today, the competence center for glass with its own teaching and experimental glassworks regularly offers more than 300 students differentiated opportunities for training and further education. Not only the profession of glassmaker is taught there, glass formers, blowers and finishers learn there, glass apparatus manufacturers, precision opticians and process mechanics, glassworks technicians; brand new is the class for product design.

Decorative leading role
Clear design and subtle color scheme - this vase leaves the dramatic appearance to your bouquet, while it resolutely yet gracefully holds your arrangement of branch and stem, leaf and flower in shape and life.
The vases are made of stoneware, i.e. sintered material, and are therefore by nature largely impermeable to water. In order to put the functional icing on the cake of this material property and at the same time enhance the aesthetic effect of form and color, the vase is painted by an experienced hand after the first firing, then glazed transparently on the outside and inside and finally fired again. The result is a subtly designed yet robust, waterproof vase that is not afraid to take a leading role on the stage of your decorations, even with long-term use.
Design meets craftsmanship. Onomao
The young Cologne-based label Onomao was born from the idea of combining traditional craftsmanship with contemporary design. When brothers Arthur and Felix Wystrychowski - one a landscape architect, the other a trained chef and graphic designer - founded their company in 2018, they were certain that their products would have as little impact on the environment as possible thanks to their long service life and short delivery routes, and that fair trade should not remain an empty phrase. With a long-standing connection to Atlantic waves, the country and its people, the two passionate surfers traveled to Portugal and went in search of people who (still) understand their craft, who work with local raw materials and carefully sourced natural materials and with whom they can implement their design ideas. This is how the brothers came across manufacturers who still rely on cultivating and preserving the regionally rooted art of pottery. The manufacture of this product is thanks to one of these tradition-conscious Portuguese craft businesses, a family company founded in the center of Portugal in 1988.

Generous, tall-format vase made of fine porcelain with filigree walls. The slender, concave shape of the vessel seems to quote the hand-painted pattern in cobalt blue - a truly beautiful combination of form and graphics. Sargadelos
Tradition and craftsmanship, a fine sense of form and coloration. Sargadelos is a ceramics company with a long history: for over 200 years, the now 200-strong company has been producing high-quality and exquisitely crafted products - including vases, bowls and tableware with finely worked graphic patterns and reliefs - in its two production facilities in Galicia, Spain. To this day, the decorations, which predominantly originate from Celtic and Galician culture, are made by hand, initially using handcrafted templates and then by hand to apply the fine details. And you can see it: the intense colors show fine gradients created by the brush application. The deep cobalt blue that characterizes many of his prints was an early trademark of the company and, in combination with the soft white tone of the ceramics, a true classic. Sargadelos became a valued reference in the world of ceramics in its early history and also attracted attention with collaborations such as the one with David Chipperfield for the REDE tableware series. Today, the Sargadelos Foundation manages the business and attaches great importance to preserving the company's cultural and artistic heritage.

product_389.description:
General Information
Recycling used glass. Vases made from wine bottles
What began two years ago in a Parisian apartment as an idea between friends is now a success story. The two Frenchmen Emeric Cruchant Fleuriau and Gauthier Decarne collect empty wine bottles to make glass flower vases in various sizes. A kind of revitalization measure, as they describe it themselves, with which they want to preserve the carefree atmosphere of wine evenings in convivial company. To this end, the two have now entered into a partnership with restaurateurs in the Hauts-de-France region, Decarne's home, who regularly hand over the used glass collected in their restaurants - more than 1,000 bottles a week - to them. The manual part of this undertaking works as follows: The bottles are first thoroughly cleaned and then the neck of the bottle is "blasted off", as they say in glass workers' jargon, i.e. first scored and then cut off with special scissors. The sharp-edged edges that are created during this process are finally sanded clean and smooth. Depending on the initial shape of the bottle and the color of the glass, the vases can turn out differently.

product_390.description:
General Information
Simple heavyweight
A strikingly straightforward simplicity characterizes these vases and lends a well-proportioned frame to any decorative idea, no matter how bold. Equally striking is their extraordinary weight, which makes it hard to believe that the vases were mouth-blown. But they were.
The designs for the glass vases come from a London design studio, a family business founded in the 1960s, which places great value on the craftsmanship of its creations as well as their functionality and modernity. And so these vases are carefully blown "in front of the lamp" in a Polish glassblowing workshop according to all the rules of traditional craftsmanship. The finish is also done by hand - until the solid wall of each of these unique pieces of craftsmanship rises straight up from a reinforced base and ends in a carefully polished upper rim. So heavy and stable, the vases are extremely versatile: They hold your arrangement of flowers, blossoms and twigs, display the finds from your walk in the woods or act as an atmospheric lantern for your pillar candle after you have filled them with a little gravel, sand or soil. And while we're on the subject of sand and soil: As a planter, the vases transform your houseplant from root to flower into a decorative object.
Note:
Certain manufacturing steps are carried out by hand. Slight dimensional and color deviations may therefore occur.

product_395.description:
General Information
Composition with the potential to become evergreen
Bouquets of flowers are something wonderful. They bring color and atmosphere into the home, they lift our spirits and add a natural finishing touch to our interior design. Especially when the bouquet in its vase retains exactly the arrangement we have thought up for it. Often, however, our creative compositions fail due to the diameter of the vase opening and the law of gravity - light bouquets fall apart into a disorderly round dance, individual flower branches only achieve the desired degree of stability by using unattractive, less water-resistant foreign materials.
The floral disk offers an attractive way out of this dilemma. Made from pure brass, it is naturally resistant to corrosion and keeps the arrangement of delicate and light bouquets in shape, even if the vase opening is a little larger. Simply place the flower disk on the opening of your vase and insert the individual stems and branches through selected holes in the disk - it will help your composition to maintain its attractive alignment and stability. And if you use one of our hand-felted new wool branches or bouquets instead of fresh cut flowers, you can even create an evergreen in your room decoration.

product_411.description:
General Information
Servant ladder
The somewhat cryptic name of this small piece of furniture - silent ladder - is decoded with the information that it is a hybrid (conceived from the ladder) of stepladder and silent servant, which is intended to fulfill both functions. In its role as a ladder, it has two steps together with a safety bar - in ladder construction, this is the name given to the combination of stiles extended in the direction of stepping and a cross connection. As a mute servant, the furniture from Auerberg in Bavaria offers space for a shirt (thrown over the top; the ash wood stiles have a semi-circular cross-section especially for this purpose) and trousers (these can be hung over the rung that cannot be stepped on). The two lower steps and a small leather-lined compartment for trouser pockets on top serve as storage areas. Further re-purposing is not excluded.
Radically simple, completely functional: furniture from Auerberg
Radical reduction in form and material and a complete focus on function - that is the guiding principle behind the furniture from Auerberg. These are handcrafted products that are designed away from industrial standards, far removed from fashion and uninfluenced by marketing constraints and produced in small batches. Behind every single piece of furniture is the authentic personality of the respective designer - and because there is no restrictive program dictate, the product designers are only committed to their own standards. Accordingly, all Auerberg furniture is unmistakable, sometimes purist to the point of stubbornness, extremely solid in terms of craftsmanship and thus virtually made to last.
The furniture is manufactured regionally in Upper Bavaria and the wood - mostly oak, ash and beech - comes from certified forestry operations. The mastermind behind Auerberg is Christoph Böninger, once a professional globetrotter, now a settled design publisher. Well-connected in design circles, Böninger works in Munich and on his farm in Auerberg - hence the name of the project - near Bad Aibling. And even though Böninger has gathered a number of designers and architects around him for his "product lab" - with established greats standing alongside up-and-coming talent - he still lends a hand himself. Sometimes he oils wooden furniture and gets it ready for shipping. Incidentally, Auerberg's greatest successes to date include the AEKI step stool by Gerhardt Kellermann and the "Silent Ladder" by Christoph Böninger himself, a versatile hybrid of stepladder and silent servant.

General Information
Hooks with a halo
The Swedish manufacturer calls its coat hook "Gloria", which translates from Swedish as "halo" (and should not be confused with the Latin "gloria", synonymous with "glory" and "honor" - although we would grant the hook this too). In fact, a halo seems to surround the hook, especially as the ring also leans into the room and casts a visually fascinating ring of shadows on the wall when the light falls on it. Beyond this, however, the design of the coat hook has little to do with holiness, but is rather the result of well thought-out reasons of functionality. Even items of clothing that lack the sewn-in loop for hanging on a hook can be stored on the ring, which is as gentle on the fabric as a coat hanger. Permanent marks and creases in the fabric are a thing of the past.
Hooks, hangers and storage in one: thanks to their high functionality in a compact form, the coat hooks are predestined to be combined into an ensemble, especially in small entrance areas and bathrooms. Each individual coat hook is made from recycled aluminum and holds many an item of clothing and shower towel securely in place. The inclined ring not only protects the cloth of your hat and coat, but is also useful as a shelf for gloves and scarves and as a clamp for all the papers and documents that you want to keep in a memorable place for the next time you go out (although we would advise against clamping your laptop, even if the load-bearing capacity of the coat hook itself would not suffer if it were mounted solidly on the wall).

Console table or shoe rack? Both!
This narrow, as simple as beautiful furniture made of oiled oak wood takes you - especially in smaller rooms - the decision whether you want to put a console table or a shoe rack, because it is both: the upper shelf end functions, for example, when using the shelf near the front door, as a shelf for everything that you should have with you when leaving the house or should not forget. product_431.description:
General Information
Simple forged wall hooks, for jackets, coats, hats. Made by Smedbo in southern Sweden.
Utility and Adornment. Furniture Fittings.
Historically, fittings were primarily intended to increase the usability of a piece of furniture; the focal point of their assessment was their practical use. Shields protected drawers, latches, corners, and edges against wear and tear in particularly stressed areas. All door knobs and drawer handles had to be particularly sturdy. The awareness of an ornamental value of such objects, on the other hand, came about later and only over the course of centuries. From the 12th century onwards, you find fittings that had a style-defining effect on their era. The Art Nouveau phase was particularly productive, creating a multitude of dainty floral décor ornaments.
European Diversity. Our Selection.
Nevertheless, the emphasis in our assortment is on the material as well as the origin of the individual articles. The century from which the design originates is less important to us. You won’t find cheap imitations from India and China in our selection; on the contrary, you will find products originating in Europe – with an emphasis on regions where the production of such fittings was traditionally at home. For example, the glass furniture knobs in our range come from a specialised glassmaking workshop in the Fichtel Mountains. One and all of our porcelain products derive from the cradle of French porcelain production, from the city of Limoges. And an iron foundry in the Ardennes provides us with the iron teacup handles. Last but not least, we have our pick’s brass furniture plates and handles made in Lüdenscheid in the Sauerland region, a traditional centre of metalworking in Germany.
Your Design Options.
You can use the fittings to embellish old furnishings or replace existing, possibly defective parts with functioning ones. Upgrade the long-cherished flea market find in a heartbeat. Deck out a self-made piece of furniture with the fittings it deserves: smooth-running castors and charming handles.

product_434.description:
General Information
Exclusive
Discover singular products that may remind you of items you already know and appreciate; however, these products – exclusively available from us – feature a refined design meeting our clear-cut requirements.
The original type. Raw iron. Hand-forged.
This is the archetype. A piece of iron, hot from the fire, worked freely with hammer blows. The path from material to form remains visible and tangible. We have this archetype of a hook made in a forge near Hamburg.
This hand-forged hook is actually made of raw, completely untreated iron. In contrast to high-alloy steels, its surface is not "fixed", it changes over the seasons, depending on humidity, temperature and simply the "passage of time". The best protection against corrosion is to grease it from time to time by holding it in your hand, which is a pleasure given the fascination of the material. Flash rust will occur if you expose the material to the weather outside (or in the bathroom); this can be easily removed with steel wool. In general, you can change the appearance of the raw iron by treating it with steel wool, sandpaper or a wire brush. Longer-lasting protection can be achieved with linseed oil, for example.

product_435.description:
General Information
Discover MAGAZIN products: Collaborating with innovative designers, MAGAZIN develops and produces this unique furniture and home accessories series.
Coat rack with an industrial character - space-creating coat rack element to combine with CONTAINER DS, CONTAINER DS AIR, CONTAINER DS with lock, CONTAINER DS FLAT or a TARA shelving unit. The coat rack itself consists of four parts and can be assembled with little effort. The fastening between the coat rack element and the containers or the shelving element is done using the enclosed connectors. The product has a hot-dip galvanized surface. The robust and industrial quality is characteristic of this type of surface finish. It is a deliberate choice and provides an exciting contrast to the painted surfaces of the containers. Max. load weight: 80 kg.
Series Container DS
Synonymous with storage and transport: the container in its archetypal surface of folded steel. We offer this cabinet furniture in the miniaturized form of overseas containers in four different versions. These well-proportioned storage boxes serve many purposes and areas of use. All containers have perforations in the bottoms for passing cables. The classic container as well as the flat and small container have doors hinged to the top of the body, which slide into the top of the body when opened and thus almost completely disappear. The CONTAINER DS PLUS is upright and has a conventional hinged door on the side.
The classic: The CONTAINER DS in the proportion of a sea container is virtually the archetype of the series CONTAINER DS. It serves as a cabinet in the living room for china and utensils for the set table, in the office for storing files in standardized format or for paper and office utensils. As a chest of drawers for linen and as a piece of furniture in the hallway and wardrobe. It can be combined in its basic rectangular shape with a variety of complementary accessories. Various feet and casters or the two framework frames serve as the basis. The shelf element TARA has the outer contour of the container and can be stacked with it in height via connectors included in the delivery. The coat rack completes the container to a functional wardrobe. The container of this format is available in limited color selection equipped with a lock. It can be mounted on the wall with a separately available bracket.
The flat one: CONTAINER DS FLAT has the footprint of the classic CONTAINER DS and can be connected to it in height and stacked. It can be combined with the above mentioned accessories of the classic CONTAINER DS. This container often serves as a flat element that is built into a stack of the classic container. It is useful with its special volume for the stack of paper, for utensils and as a shelf for many purposes. It can be mounted on the wall with a separately available bracket.
The small one: The CONTAINER DS KLEIN as the little brother of the CONTAINER DS does not have the proportions of a sea container, unlike its archetypal big role model - it is narrower, with identical depth and height. With its small size and unusual formatting, it serves as a piece of side furniture next to the bed and sofa and can also be stacked up to form a tower. It can be equipped with all separate feet as well as the casters. Unlike its sister models, it is always equipped with a smooth cover shelf in the respective color. The shelf element TARA KLEIN has the outer contour of the container and can be stacked with it in height via connectors included in the delivery.
The big one: A very special piece of furniture with its own range of uses is the CONTAINER DS PLUS. It can be used in portrait format and serves as a locker-like clothes or wardrobe cabinet and can also be used as a large-volume cabinet, individually or stacked on top of each other in the kitchen, office or other places. This large container is stackable like all other sister models via included square connectors. A clothes rail is included, and a specially designed shelf and cover shelf are available separately as accessories.
Note:
The connectors are supplied with all DS series containers and the TARA and TARA KLEIN shelving units. They only need to be purchased separately when used in conjunction with two or more scaffolding frames or coat racks.

product_447.description:
General Information
Lovely for the love of order
Mine! People of all ages who live in a community enjoy being together - and at the same time having their own personal (free) space. With a children's wardrobe mounted at a child-friendly low level, you can create a dedicated area for your child in the hallway, which they can and may use independently and with pride of ownership. In the playful ritual of dressing and undressing, the children's wardrobe encourages your offspring to store their jacket, scarf and gym bag in such a way that they can be (and remain) found and within easy reach. And since the willingness to keep things tidy is also much easier (and more lasting) to achieve through a positive affect, the lovable, cheerful and colorful design of the wardrobe caterpillar also promotes children's love of order. This is even possible in the long term, as the solid softwood construction "endures" even hanging up and taking out with lasting solidity, even if the child has no motor skills.
Exemplarily unique. Margarete Ostheimer
Of course there is a pattern - more precisely, a template designed in-house, according to which the Ostheimer wooden toys are made. And yet, on the way from the design to the finished product, each figure develops into a small one-off. This is because the company has always attached great importance to the high quality of its toys: from careful sawing out, which takes into account the grain of the wood, to rough and fine sanding and painting by hand, they are made by skilled craftsmen. In many individual steps, wooden toys are created that encourage your child to play freely, lively and imaginatively.
In Zell unter Aichelberg in Baden-Württemberg, Margarete Ostheimer GmbH pays attention to sustainable manufacturing processes, which is why only wood from regional forestry is used in the European partner companies. The company is also committed to social issues and promotes social interaction, for example by setting up integrative workplaces for people with support needs. In addition, Ostheimer Holzspielzeug is owned by the Ostheimer Foundation, which was established in 2001 and supports social projects and initiatives with the profits generated.
Note:
Certain manufacturing steps are carried out by hand. Slight dimensional and color deviations may therefore occur.

product_449.description:
General Information
Discover MAGAZIN products: Collaborating with innovative designers, MAGAZIN develops and produces this unique furniture and home accessories series.
The coat rack is now also available for the CONTAINER DS KLEIN and the TARA KLEIN shelving unit. The result is a space-creating wardrobe with an industrial character - even for narrow rooms and niches. The coat rack itself consists of four parts and can be assembled with little effort. It is attached between the coat rack element and the containers or shelving element using the enclosed connectors. The product has a hot-dip galvanized surface. The robust and industrial quality is characteristic of this type of surface finish. It is a deliberate choice and provides an exciting contrast to the painted surfaces of the containers. Max. load weight: 80 kg.
Series Container DS
Synonymous with storage and transport: the container in its archetypal surface of folded steel. We offer this cabinet furniture in the miniaturized form of overseas containers in four different versions. These well-proportioned storage boxes serve many purposes and areas of use. All containers have perforations in the bottoms for passing cables. The classic container as well as the flat and small container have doors hinged to the top of the body, which slide into the top of the body when opened and thus almost completely disappear. The CONTAINER DS PLUS is upright and has a conventional hinged door on the side.
The classic: The CONTAINER DS in the proportion of a sea container is virtually the archetype of the series CONTAINER DS. It serves as a cabinet in the living room for china and utensils for the set table, in the office for storing files in standardized format or for paper and office utensils. As a chest of drawers for linen and as a piece of furniture in the hallway and wardrobe. It can be combined in its basic rectangular shape with a variety of complementary accessories. Various feet and casters or the two framework frames serve as the basis. The shelf element TARA has the outer contour of the container and can be stacked with it in height via connectors included in the delivery. The coat rack completes the container to a functional wardrobe. The container of this format is available in limited color selection equipped with a lock. It can be mounted on the wall with a separately available bracket.
The flat one: CONTAINER DS FLAT has the footprint of the classic CONTAINER DS and can be connected to it in height and stacked. It can be combined with the above mentioned accessories of the classic CONTAINER DS. This container often serves as a flat element that is built into a stack of the classic container. It is useful with its special volume for the stack of paper, for utensils and as a shelf for many purposes. It can be mounted on the wall with a separately available bracket.
The small one: The CONTAINER DS KLEIN as the little brother of the CONTAINER DS does not have the proportions of a sea container, unlike its archetypal big role model - it is narrower, with identical depth and height. With its small size and unusual formatting, it serves as a piece of side furniture next to the bed and sofa and can also be stacked up to form a tower. It can be equipped with all separate feet as well as the casters. Unlike its sister models, it is always equipped with a smooth cover shelf in the respective color. The shelf element TARA KLEIN has the outer contour of the container and can be stacked with it in height via connectors included in the delivery.
The big one: A very special piece of furniture with its own range of uses is the CONTAINER DS PLUS. It can be used in portrait format and serves as a locker-like clothes or wardrobe cabinet and can also be used as a large-volume cabinet, individually or stacked on top of each other in the kitchen, office or other places. This large container is stackable like all other sister models via included square connectors. A clothes rail is included, and a specially designed shelf and cover shelf are available separately as accessories.
Note:
The connectors are supplied with all DS series containers and the TARA and TARA KLEIN shelving units. They only need to be purchased separately when used in conjunction with two or more scaffolding frames or coat racks.

product_453.description:
General Information
Children's clothes hanger made of solid beech wood. Just like for the grown-ups
Tidiness is half the battle - that's something even the offspring will (have to) learn at some point, and also that this applies not only to the toys in the children's room, but also in the closet and on the coat rack - at least adults appreciate this very much. One hurdle (among many) in this regard are the organizational utensils that, while helpful, are designed entirely for adults in terms of format. Unhandy, large and heavy, small children's hands can hardly handle them well - how can they enjoy tidying up and neatly hanging away clothes that, once they are finally on the hanger, sit stretched out strangely. How much more fun it is to be able to use the same, but child-friendly tidying aids when the same tidying duties apply.
These hangers for children are therefore adapted in size to children's sweaters and jackets, but otherwise just as solidly manufactured as the hangers for adults: made of solid, steamed beech wood, which is sanded several times, additionally smoothed and finally varnished. Thus, the hangers not only support children's clothing, but can also be used later or in parallel for smaller women's shirts and t-shirts. Each hanger is equipped with a sturdy, nickel-plated hook. We offer the children's hanger in a set of three.

product_456.description:
General Information
Reduced to the bare essentials in terms of form and materials - a wall hook can not be simpler and more restrained and thus fits into any bathroom.
Asketic: Bathroom utensils made of ring and rod
The utensils, designed by architect Theo Keller, are manufactured in a locksmith's shop in southern Germany with a high proportion of handicraft work.
The principle: all utensils - from the towel bar to the soap holder to the toilet paper holder - are made from the same workpiece, a stainless steel rod 8 mm in diameter, by bending, folding and turning. The only fastening element is a ring manufactured on the lathe, also made of stainless steel and fitted with a wall screw; other parts such as covers or similar are superfluous. The ring provides fixed or movable storage for the various items, either individually or in pairs. For fixed storage, it is equipped with an additional hole and a hexagon socket grub screw.
The designer himself provides his bathroom series with the attributes "final, timeless, ascetic". We would have nothing to add to that.
Finally, the Design Center of North Rhine-Westphalia recognized the quality of this design in 2004 with the Red Dot Award for product design, one of the most important prizes for good design.

product_474.description:
General Information
For coats or towels
This swivel hook made of polished aluminum is simply classified by the manufacturer as a triple coat hook. It is only suitable for underneath mounting - under the hat shelf in the hallway perhaps or under the kitchen worktop. Instead of coats and jackets, the lightweight hook can also hold tea towels and oven mitts as required. We source it from Hermann Schwerter in Iserlohn, a hardware dealer since 1905 and today one of the last remaining producers of fittings and coat racks in the region, which was once famous for its metalworking tradition.
Utility and Adornment. Furniture Fittings.
Historically, fittings were primarily intended to increase the usability of a piece of furniture; the focal point of their assessment was their practical use. Shields protected drawers, latches, corners, and edges against wear and tear in particularly stressed areas. All door knobs and drawer handles had to be particularly sturdy. The awareness of an ornamental value of such objects, on the other hand, came about later and only over the course of centuries. From the 12th century onwards, you find fittings that had a style-defining effect on their era. The Art Nouveau phase was particularly productive, creating a multitude of dainty floral décor ornaments.
European Diversity. Our Selection.
Nevertheless, the emphasis in our assortment is on the material as well as the origin of the individual articles. The century from which the design originates is less important to us. You won’t find cheap imitations from India and China in our selection; on the contrary, you will find products originating in Europe – with an emphasis on regions where the production of such fittings was traditionally at home. For example, the glass furniture knobs in our range come from a specialised glassmaking workshop in the Fichtel Mountains. One and all of our porcelain products derive from the cradle of French porcelain production, from the city of Limoges. And an iron foundry in the Ardennes provides us with the iron teacup handles. Last but not least, we have our pick’s brass furniture plates and handles made in Lüdenscheid in the Sauerland region, a traditional centre of metalworking in Germany.
Your Design Options.
You can use the fittings to embellish old furnishings or replace existing, possibly defective parts with functioning ones. Upgrade the long-cherished flea market find in a heartbeat. Deck out a self-made piece of furniture with the fittings it deserves: smooth-running castors and charming handles.

product_476.description:
General Information
Solid tea towel. Classic herringbone pattern
This tea towel woven in a herringbone pattern comes from the traditional Framsohn weaving mill in the Waldviertel region of Lower Austria. Since 1908, all production steps have been carried out under one roof. The soft cotton fabric is highly absorbent with a medium material weight of 260 g/sqm and can absorb a lot of moisture. The sturdy cloth can also be used for hands during kitchen operations.
Framsohn. Terry goods and home textiles from the Waldviertel region
Framsohn, the name stands for Franz Amstetter & Söhne, in the Waldviertel region of Lower Austria, is a fourth-generation manufacturer of high-quality home textiles and terry towelling. The family business has always attached great importance to its connection with nature and the local people. This attitude is reflected in several factors. For example, Framsohn weaves the terry towelling from organic-certified cotton. All production still takes place at the company's original headquarters. This reduces transportation routes, allows continuous quality control from the thread to the finished product and enables Framsohn to influence all parameters directly and immediately. To document this, Framsohn has been certified in accordance with the Global Organic Textile Standard (GOTS). This sets high standards for the production of textiles made from organically produced natural fibers - across the entire production chain: from the extraction of textile fibers, through their processing and distribution, to ethical and social criteria. Compliance with the standard is reviewed annually and the GOTS certification is re-awarded.

product_479.description:
General Information
Colorful tea towel with a complex pattern. The non-slip cotton fabric is made exclusively from yarn remnants from the textile industry, combines different weave structures and brings color into the kitchen.
Odds & Ends
Colorful home textiles made from industrial waste! When factories dye yarn to weave textiles, they often produce more yarn than is needed - just in case. This means that considerable quantities of yarn are regularly left over, which are normally disposed of. For the textiles in the Odds & Ends collection, Foekje Fleur collects these yarn remnants - exclusively cotton yarns - and uses them to produce home textiles. Dishcloths, dishcloths, washcloths and shower towels in predetermined complex, graphic patterns of overlapping and intersecting lines in different colors and thicknesses. Their colors are created depending on the yarns available. And in batches: after sifting through the available yarns, the Dutch designer puts together the eye-catching and finely balanced color combinations for the next batch of the collection. If the yarns run out, individual colors are replaced or a completely new combination is created. Small variations in the color scheme within a batch are therefore planned for, as are slight differences in size due to production. Odds & Ends scarves are made in Portugal and are easily recognizable by their striped hems woven on a jacquard machine. Practically all of the scarves have a hanger and are quick-drying. The exceptionally beautifully designed hangers and banderoles with which the scarves are supplied are the work of Dutch illustrator Rachel Sender and make the scarves the ideal gift.
Hint:

product_480.description:
General Information
This pit towel in the original version with the black and gray checkered pattern and the surrounding red stripes was rarely available. The Leinenweberei Vieböck in the Austrian Mühlviertel weaves it again - especially for Manufactum.
As black as coal dust
Once upon a time, no miner's washroom was complete without it: the pit towel, which the miners used to dry themselves off and which had to be black in pattern because it made coal dust invisible. The black and grey checked pattern was characteristic, but for a long time the pit towel was only available as a blue checked tea towel. For many years, we had the original in black specially made again by the Hessian linen weaving mill Driessen. The news that the owner would be retiring in 2024 therefore hit us hard, all the more so because he had been unable to find a successor - the weaving mill would be closed and all production discontinued.
What now? A home textiles range without this pit cloth is possible, but pointless. So we looked for a weaving mill that could reweave this cloth for us. The chances were good, as we had often realized our own developments with some of our suppliers - mostly small to medium-sized companies. We therefore asked Vieböck, an Austrian linen weaving mill with tradition and experience. They were immediately enthusiastic about our pit cloth - and the quality of its material and workmanship. They set to work with the aim of producing something at least as good. We, in turn, are delighted with the result: we cannot see any difference to the original and are extremely pleased to be able to continue offering you the black checked pit towel.
As before, it is woven in a twill weave - i.e. with red stripes all around - in a non-slip and hard-wearing twisted half-linen quality made of cotton twine (Nm 70/2) in the warp and linen twine (Nm 26/2) in the weft with a basis weight of 270 g/sqm. A home textile range without this fabric is possible, but not necessary ...

product_485.description:
General Information
Solid all-rounder. Durable and functional
This tea towel is classically made from absorbent cotton. Woven in solid full-twist quality (Nm 34/2) and in a tight plain weave, it proves to be a durable workhorse in the kitchen, from drying dishes and pots to covering dough. And as robust as the fabric is, the tea towel is just as hard-wearing thanks to the coloring: stains seem to disappear almost without a trace on the dark blue background - all those who have a lot to do with tomato sauce or beet in the kitchen will appreciate this.
Woven goods from Upper Austria: known for centuries
The good reputation of the Mühlviertel weaving trade was already established around 1600 and in many communities, half of the inhabitants earned their income from weaving or related occupations. The raw material used by the weavers was flax, which was widely cultivated in the Mühlviertel at the time. At the time, weaving products were one of Upper Austria's most important exports. Since around 1700, strict quality and control regulations have ensured compliance with high quality standards. Standards that the traditional Vieböck weaving mill still works to today.
The yarn count
We specify the yarn count in Nm (metric number), whereby the higher the number, the finer the yarn. A yarn count of Nm 100 means that 100 meters of yarn weigh 1 gram. An additional number is added if the yarn is twisted from several single yarns, for example Nm 100/3 for a twisted yarn made from three single yarns.

product_488.product_name: Glass cloth linen jacquard, Slate Grey
product_488.alt_text: Glass cloth linen jacquard, Slate Grey
product_488.description:
General Information
The best for glasses. Pure linen
For drying glasses, especially fine champagne and wine glasses, hardly any material is more suitable than linen. It dries very well, is hard-wearing and low in lint, but above all it does not cling to the glass wall, as often happens with cotton cloths.
Le Jacquard Français uses pure linen, woven from fine long flax yarns, for the smooth glass cloth with its intricate jacquard pattern. The high-quality yarns ensure that the dense, tight jacquard fabric gets a beautiful "luster" and shimmers typical of linen.
Traditional Weaving in the Vosges. Le Jacquard Français.
Besides fine natural materials, lively patterns and daring colour combinations characterise the table linen and bathroom textiles from Le Jacquard Français. It hadn’t always been like that: Until the 1970s, home textiles were primarily white. That’s why the weaving mill, initially founded in 1861 as a drapery business, originally produced a wide range of textile goods – made of cotton, linen and half-linen – in white – the more so since Le Jacquard Français set up its own bleaching plant in 1928. At the same time, the mill invested in acquisitions of modern Jacquard looms and specialised in weaving high-quality damask fabrics with the pattern visible on both the front and back. The Jacquard looms allow for a complex, automated weaving technique and the application of several different weaves for one fabric. The technical capability of the looms provides the set-up for motifs that are as complex as they are varied. Nowadays, the company operates on a fully integrated basis at its headquarters in Gérardemer: from spinning to weaving and refining to dressing and finishing. With 54 Jacquard looms, 120 employees and the experience of well over a century, Le Jacquard Français is now one of France’s traditional companies. The French Ministry of Economy awarded the mill Entreprise du Patrimoine Vivant (i. e. Living Heritage in English). Combining traditional handicraft and technological innovation is especially characteristic of the mill’s production processes – particularly evident in the dyeing process at Le Jacquard Français, and for a good reason.
In Style and Striking Colours. From Trousseaus to Fashion Accessories.
When Le Jacquard Français brought the famous designer Primrose Bordier on board in 1978, it marked a turning point in the brand’s history. Bordier broke with the conventions in home textile designs and breathed life into the traditional ornamentation. While home textiles came until then dominantly in plain white, his designs surprised with imaginative patterns and intense, bright colours. Le Jacquard Français invests again, this time in colour research, and brings a wind of change to the industry with its colourful collections. Its trousseau pieces become fashion accessories and style elements for interior designs – and Le Jacquard Français becomes an international player among textile manufacturers.
The French mill chooses high-quality, long-staple fibres for spinning. The fineness and superior quality of the resulting cotton and linen yarns are the essential factors when it comes to the intense colours and the shine and precision of the motifs. Le Jacquard Français received the Masters of Linen® label, a quality award for linen 100 per cent produced in Europe: from the harvest and the fibre up to the finished fabric.

Kenya's colors in Finnish weaving tradition
Lapuan Kankurit, a weaving mill based in the small western Finnish town of Lapua, specializes in linen and jacquard fabrics. For this pure linen tea towel, Lapuan has teamed up with Mifuko, another Finnish label, whose designs are inspired by Kenyan tradition and craftsmanship. This stems from the long-standing ties of the two designers with Kenya, which eventually led to a cooperation with Kenyan craftswomen.
The cloth owes its design and cheerful colors to this Kenyan influence, because in the natural white base are woven different widths, yarn-dyed stripes. The linen is woven in twill weave and washed on the spot after being made up, giving it a soft handle and a lively structure - but also making it impossible to iron perfectly smooth. Only the best linen yarns from long-fiber flax of European provenance are woven on the looms of the company, which is now in its fourth generation. General Information
Linen Cloth. For tableware and color accent
From the Finnish linen and jacquard weaving company Lapuan Kankurit, we source these tea towels with different colored sides. Made of pure linen, they are absorbent, grippy and durable. Due to their medium material weight of 250 g/sqm, they are suitable not only for dishes but also as hand towels. Lapuan Kankurit weaves the tea towels like a doubleface with two colors: with natural-colored yarn in the warp and colored yarn in the weft. This creates different colored sides, so you can use the towels to create a colorful accent in your kitchen, depending on your mood.
The weaving mill uses only the best linen yarns from long fiber flax of European provenance, including for these tea towels. That they are woven on a shuttle loom is evidenced by their selvedges on the long sides. They are created when the loom is set up specifically for the width of the woven material and the weft thread is not simply cut off, but continued endlessly. Thus, only the upper and lower cut edge must be hemmed.

The set contains two tea towels. The motifs - a large stag on one, many small stags on the other - are woven in. The tea towels are only available in this set from Manufactum.
The stag in the kitchen
The elephant in the china store, the dog in the pan ... we thought there was still a stag missing in the kitchen! The stag found its way into our range via our Viennese department store. Framsohn visited us there for an event and brought along a whole bunch of these tea towel sets. It was so well received by our Austrian customers that it not only sold out in no time at all, but was also in constant demand. So we are now providing supplies directly via our store so that the woven deer can now also romp around in your kitchen.
As we have come to expect from Framsohn textiles, the tea towel has the right practical properties for working in the kitchen: Woven from soft cotton, it is hard-wearing and at the same time supple, with a medium material weight of 250 g/sqm it is also highly absorbent and can absorb a lot of moisture. This means that the solid cloth not only dries dishes, but can also be used for hands in the kitchen.
Framsohn. Terry goods and home textiles from the Waldviertel region
Framsohn, the name stands for Franz Amstetter & Söhne, in the Waldviertel region of Lower Austria, is a fourth-generation manufacturer of high-quality home textiles and terry towelling. The family business has always attached great importance to its connection with nature and the local people. This attitude is reflected in several factors. For example, Framsohn weaves the terry towelling from organic-certified cotton. All production still takes place at the company's original headquarters. This reduces transportation routes, allows continuous quality control from the thread to the finished product and enables Framsohn to influence all parameters directly and immediately. To document this, Framsohn has been certified in accordance with the Global Organic Textile Standard (GOTS). This sets high standards for the production of textiles made from organically produced natural fibers - across the entire production chain: from the extraction of textile fibers, through their processing and distribution, to ethical and social criteria. Compliance with the standard is reviewed annually and the GOTS certification is re-awarded.

A special kind of tea towel is this one from Erika Vaitkute's linen weaving mill: with its unusual blue and red check pattern on the natural-colored background, it is already an eye-catcher in the kitchen. And even though the plaid looks traditional, it's a more recent design, as is the edging of the edges in light blue, which adds an eye-catching detail. Woven from pure European linen, it's absorbent, grippy and durable, and as is typical of linen, gets softer with each wash. With a basis weight of 210 g/sqm, it is not only suitable for drying dishes, but is a real all-rounder in your kitchen.
Passion for Lithuanian linen. Erika Vaitkute
Erika Vaitkute has been passionate about textiles and fabrics, especially linen, for as long as she can remember. From a young age, she sewed with her mother, who also taught her to appreciate Lithuanian linen. It is important to know that Lithuania has a living and deeply rooted linen tradition dating back thousands of years - it is therefore not unusual for Lithuanians to engage with and continue old textile techniques. On the contrary, in recent years there has been a strong resurgence of interest in them, both throughout the Baltic States and among young artists, designers and craftspeople.
In the meantime, Erika Vaitkute's path (and her sewing machine) has taken her to Germany, but her passion for fine linen textiles and the traditional craft behind them has remained. So she set up a small studio in Hamburg, where she and her team design the patterns and collections. However, the fabrics are still woven and made up in her manufactory in Lithuania. According to all the rules of Lithuanian linen weaving, sophisticated handcrafted pieces are created there, from table linen to hand and kitchen towels to blankets. Only the best linen from long-fiber flax of European origin is used. This not only guarantees the high quality of the linen, but also the careful processing of the ancient crop under fair conditions.

Design with function. "Caring is the new cool"

To achieve this, founder Joy Vasiljev only uses cotton from controlled organic cultivation for her textiles. The designs are created in collaboration with Danish textile designers - always with the aim of making the textiles so well thought-out and appealing that they are enjoyed and, above all, used for a long time.

product_500.description:
General Information
The best for glasses. Pure linen
For drying glasses, especially fine champagne and wine glasses, hardly any material is more suitable than linen. It dries very well, is hard-wearing and low in lint, but above all it does not cling to the glass wall, as often happens with cotton cloths.
Le Jacquard Français uses pure linen, woven from fine long flax yarns, for the smooth glass cloth with its intricate jacquard pattern. The high-quality yarns ensure that the dense, tight jacquard fabric gets a beautiful "luster" and shimmers typical of linen.
Traditional Weaving in the Vosges. Le Jacquard Français.
Besides fine natural materials, lively patterns and daring colour combinations characterise the table linen and bathroom textiles from Le Jacquard Français. It hadn’t always been like that: Until the 1970s, home textiles were primarily white. That’s why the weaving mill, initially founded in 1861 as a drapery business, originally produced a wide range of textile goods – made of cotton, linen and half-linen – in white – the more so since Le Jacquard Français set up its own bleaching plant in 1928. At the same time, the mill invested in acquisitions of modern Jacquard looms and specialised in weaving high-quality damask fabrics with the pattern visible on both the front and back. The Jacquard looms allow for a complex, automated weaving technique and the application of several different weaves for one fabric. The technical capability of the looms provides the set-up for motifs that are as complex as they are varied. Nowadays, the company operates on a fully integrated basis at its headquarters in Gérardemer: from spinning to weaving and refining to dressing and finishing. With 54 Jacquard looms, 120 employees and the experience of well over a century, Le Jacquard Français is now one of France’s traditional companies. The French Ministry of Economy awarded the mill Entreprise du Patrimoine Vivant (i. e. Living Heritage in English). Combining traditional handicraft and technological innovation is especially characteristic of the mill’s production processes – particularly evident in the dyeing process at Le Jacquard Français, and for a good reason.
In Style and Striking Colours. From Trousseaus to Fashion Accessories.
When Le Jacquard Français brought the famous designer Primrose Bordier on board in 1978, it marked a turning point in the brand’s history. Bordier broke with the conventions in home textile designs and breathed life into the traditional ornamentation. While home textiles came until then dominantly in plain white, his designs surprised with imaginative patterns and intense, bright colours. Le Jacquard Français invests again, this time in colour research, and brings a wind of change to the industry with its colourful collections. Its trousseau pieces become fashion accessories and style elements for interior designs – and Le Jacquard Français becomes an international player among textile manufacturers.
The French mill chooses high-quality, long-staple fibres for spinning. The fineness and superior quality of the resulting cotton and linen yarns are the essential factors when it comes to the intense colours and the shine and precision of the motifs. Le Jacquard Français received the Masters of Linen® label, a quality award for linen 100 per cent produced in Europe: from the harvest and the fibre up to the finished fabric.

Linen Cloth. For tableware and color accent
From the Finnish linen and jacquard weaving company Lapuan Kankurit, we source these tea towels with different colored sides. Made of pure linen, they are absorbent, grippy and durable. Due to their medium material weight of 250 g/sqm, they are suitable not only for dishes but also as hand towels. Lapuan Kankurit weaves the tea towels like a doubleface with two colors: with natural-colored yarn in the warp and colored yarn in the weft. This creates different colored sides, so you can use the towels to create a colorful accent in your kitchen, depending on your mood.
The weaving mill uses only the best linen yarns from long fiber flax of European provenance, including for these tea towels. That they are woven on a shuttle loom is evidenced by their selvedges on the long sides. They are created when the loom is set up specifically for the width of the woven material and the weft thread is not simply cut off, but continued endlessly. Thus, only the upper and lower cut edge must be hemmed.

product_502.description:
General Information
For dishes and the kitchen
This tea towel is a real workhorse in your kitchen, classically woven from cotton in full-twist quality and plain weave: from drying dishes and pots to covering dough. With a material weight of 165 g/sqm, it has high absorbency and is robust and hard-wearing thanks to the use of strong cotton yarn (Nm 34/2) in the warp and weft. The tea towel with a lilac background provides a friendly splash of color in the kitchen, while the light grey version blends in discreetly everywhere. The fine check pattern in white is woven into both.
Woven goods from Upper Austria: known for centuries
The good reputation of the Mühlviertel weaving trade was already established around 1600 and in many communities, half of the inhabitants earned their income from weaving or related occupations. The raw material used by the weavers was flax, which was widely cultivated in the Mühlviertel at the time. At the time, weaving products were one of Upper Austria's most important exports. Since around 1700, strict quality and control regulations have ensured compliance with high quality standards. Standards that the traditional Vieböck weaving mill still works to today.
The yarn count
We specify the yarn count in Nm (metric number), whereby the higher the number, the finer the yarn. A yarn count of Nm 100 means that 100 meters of yarn weigh 1 gram. An additional number is added if the yarn is twisted from several single yarns, for example Nm 100/3 for a twisted yarn made from three single yarns.

product_504.description:
General Information
Exclusive
The set contains two tea towels. The motifs - a large stag on one, many small stags on the other - are woven in. The tea towels are only available in this set from Manufactum.
The stag in the kitchen
The elephant in the china store, the dog in the pan ... we thought there was still a stag missing in the kitchen! The stag found its way into our range via our Viennese department store. Framsohn visited us there for an event and brought along a whole bunch of these tea towel sets. It was so well received by our Austrian customers that it not only sold out in no time at all, but was also in constant demand. So we are now providing supplies directly via our store so that the woven deer can now also romp around in your kitchen.
As we have come to expect from Framsohn textiles, the tea towel has the right practical properties for working in the kitchen: Woven from soft cotton, it is hard-wearing and at the same time supple, with a medium material weight of 250 g/sqm it is also highly absorbent and can absorb a lot of moisture. This means that the solid cloth not only dries dishes, but can also be used for hands in the kitchen.
Framsohn. Terry goods and home textiles from the Waldviertel region
Framsohn, the name stands for Franz Amstetter & Söhne, in the Waldviertel region of Lower Austria, is a fourth-generation manufacturer of high-quality home textiles and terry towelling. The family business has always attached great importance to its connection with nature and the local people. This attitude is reflected in several factors. For example, Framsohn weaves the terry towelling from organic-certified cotton. All production still takes place at the company's original headquarters. This reduces transportation routes, allows continuous quality control from the thread to the finished product and enables Framsohn to influence all parameters directly and immediately. To document this, Framsohn has been certified in accordance with the Global Organic Textile Standard (GOTS). This sets high standards for the production of textiles made from organically produced natural fibers - across the entire production chain: from the extraction of textile fibers, through their processing and distribution, to ethical and social criteria. Compliance with the standard is reviewed annually and the GOTS certification is re-awarded.

Made from strong, hard-wearing half-linen and slightly thicker in the weave (surface weight 250 g/sqm), this tea towel also dries larger quantities. It can therefore also be used as a kitchen towel: for wet hands, hot pots or clean worktops.

The stripes and the surrounding frame are jacquard woven and therefore appear on the reverse of the cloth in the same color. We recommend allowing the tea towel to dry well after use, preferably spread out over a towel rail or line.

product_511.description:
General Information
Kitchen towel made of strong linen. For hands and pots
The French weaving mill Charvet uses strong, undyed linen yarn of Nm 6 for this robust, plain weave kitchen towel. This makes it very durable and gives it a robust feel. Thanks to its generous material weight of 382 g/sqm, it is extremely absorbent and - when folded twice or three times - can even replace a potholder. The edge strips with the small-scale cube pattern are jacquard woven. The cloth is pre-washed, which means that linen fabric is already somewhat more supple and shrinkage is only around 3%. We recommend using detergents without optical brighteners so that the natural shade is retained for a long time.
Toiles de Cuisine. Dish Towels Made in France.
The Charvet weaving mill’s history started more than 100 years ago in the small town of Armentières, on the border with Flanders. Still based in the middle of one of the traditional flax-growing regions in Europe, Charvet specializes in linen and cotton fabrics production. Their range includes the robust linen fabrics that were once essential textiles for bakeries (toiles de boulangerie) and French workwear (for example, “vareuses” or pea jackets for fishermen), as well as tent tarpaulins and sailcloth fabrics besides kitchen towels.

product_522.description:
General Information
Practical version of the original: In 1965, in Egon Eiermann's environment, a dismountable version of the original Eiermann table frame was created in the locksmith's shop at Karlsruhe University of Applied Sciences - an interpretation that was not Egon Eiermann's own idea, but was initiated by one of his assistants. Unlike the original, the cross does not sit in the sloping space, but at right angles between the side sections. The cross brace tubes are bolted together back to back and to the side sections via the tube segments welded to their ends. A practical side effect: by raising the cross struts, more storage and leg space is created under the table top. The height and angle of the table top can be individually adjusted using the extension rods supplied: The rods are 33.5 cm long, have 5 adjustment options and allow working heights from 72 cm to 86 cm. If two of the rods are set higher than the other two, the table top can also be set at an angle. We offer the frame with an eccentrically positioned cross, including long extension rods and rubber stoppers.
Egon Eiermann - architect and designer
Egon Fritz Wilhelm Eiermann, born in Neuendorf near Berlin in 1904, is considered one of the most important German architects of post-war modernism. His residential buildings from the 1930s, the handkerchief weaving mill in Blumberg in 1951, St. Matthew's Church in Pforzheim in 1953, the German Pavilion at the World Exhibition in Brussels in 1958, the new Kaiser Wilhelm Memorial Church in Berlin in 1961, the German Embassy in Washington in 1964, the high-rise parliament building in Bonn in 1969 and the administration buildings for IBM and Olivetti in Stuttgart and Frankfurt in 1970 are among his most important buildings.Eiermann was a full professor at the Faculty of Architecture at the Technical University in Karlsruhe, where he ran his own architectural practice and also designed numerous pieces of furniture during this time. These included his archetypal tubular steel table frame in 1953, with whose reduced construction Eiermann - coming from the field of architecture - found the optimum combination of material use and stability. Designed as a work table that could not be dismantled, the original served as the basis for various further developments. In 1965, for example, a demountable version with a decentrally mounted and vertically aligned cross was created, followed later by a version that can also be used as a dining table and a small version for children by manufacturer Richard Lampert and in exchange with Eiermann's descendants.

product_525.description:
General Information
Master of the Chair.
Hans J. Wegner (1914-2007) designed more than 500 chairs in his long professional life earning him the title “Master of the Chair”. Wegner is undisputedly the great figure of modern Scandinavian furniture design. Renowned Design museums like the MoMa in New York and the Neue Sammlung in Munich present complete series of his chairs. So much for the mark, he left in design history. His organically shaped, exquisite chairs, preferably made of light wood, set the tone in Scandinavian furniture design for decades; today, they enjoy almost archetypal status. Contemporary Scandinavian seating furniture seems to stem from these furnishing forefathers, although some of the children and children’s children bear a suspiciously strong resemblance to Wegner’s designs.
Wegner’s CH24 – The “Y-Chair”.
Admittedly, even the CH24 has ancestors. The chair is one of Wegner’s designs that owe their shape to his preoccupation with Chinese furniture construction. The seating furniture of the late Ming dynasty inspired him when he found the furnishings characterised by precisely what he tried to realise in his model chairs: a restrained-to-the-max design vocabulary and constructions that combine optimum stability with comfortable sitting. He took the basic idea of the Chinese Quanyi (internationally known as the “Horseshoe Chair”, recognisable by its strictly rectangular seat and its back and armrest curved like a horseshoe) and varied the design by inserting a filigree yet sufficiently stabilising Y-shaped element in place of the broad backrest-supporting backboard typical of the Quanyi. The CH24, however, is far more than a mere variation of a Chinese piece of furniture: To begin with, the construction of the substructure is unmistakably Scandinavian and lightweight. Furthermore, Wegner, who was always open to new, unusual materials, had the seat woven by hand from 120 metres of paper cord. The design of the CH24 dates back to 1949 and is by far Wegner’s most successful one. The chair, meanwhile well-known as the “Y-chair “or “Wishbone chair”, has been produced since 1950 – and still is – by Carl Hansen & Søn in Gelstedt near Odense. The Danes manufacture the classic chair – the process consists of more than 100 individual steps – in a number of pieces that keeps the price well below that of comparable style icons (and other Wegner models).
Light, strong and comfortable. Three classic chairs.
“A chair is a complicated object. Anyone who has ever tried to design a chair knows that. There are endless possibilities and many problems – a chair has to be lightweight, it has to be sturdy and comfortable at the same time. It is almost easier to build a skyscraper than a chair,” said Mies van der Rohe (1886-1969). As is well known, it did not stop him from designing chairs (and creating some classics in the process, most notably the Barcelona Chair in 1929). Nevertheless, his statement hits a nerve: the challenge he faced in the process is one that everyone is prone to discover who tries the same. And if, on top, a basic design idea – an aesthetic demand – goes into the mix, it becomes all the more complicated. Eventually, it is no surprise that the furniture market produces numerous “new” chairs year after year, but lasting classics are extremely rare among them.
We offer three models from a period that was very productive in this respect: the late 1940s and early 1950s. On the one hand, they represent (in the case of the “Y-Chair” or “Wishbone Chair” by the Dane Hans J. Wegner) the independent tradition of modern Scandinavian furniture design. On the other hand (in the case of Egon Eiermann’s chairs), they stand for the so-called “Second Modernism”. In post-war Germany, the design approach – and Egon Eiermann as a leading protagonist – successfully reclaimed the legacy of modern furniture design of the 1910s and 1920s Werkbund and Bauhaus design schools.
